player.seasonOutlook: Fantasy managers have been (im)patiently awaiting the return of Guerrero's 2021 AL MVP runner-up form. When he finally displayed it, it was during a time when few could reap the rewards. We're talking the 2025 playoffs, where he hit .397/.494/.795 with eight homers in 18 games. That's not to substantially knock Guerrero for his regular-season exploits, as the past five seasons have seen him post the fifth-most fantasy-point average (478.6), the second-most total hits (893) and third-most total bases (1,546). He's a model of consistency with a star's ability to shine at any moment, even if those are sometimes seemingly selective. Still a prime-age 27, Guerrero should be one of your first couple of picks, even if he's not necessarily worthy of being the first.

Chisholm and Yankee Stadium represented the perfect marriage, as his first full season in pinstripes saw him pull a career-high 53.3% of batted balls and hit 33.2% in the air (his second-highest single year rate), resulting in his first 30/30 campaign. It did, however, cost him in batting average, as his .242 was his full-season worst, putting more emphasis on his need to steal bases to make up the difference for fantasy. Chisholm's declining speed metrics, and the groin issue that made him more conservative on the basepaths around midseason, raise slight concerns, but he's still one of the better early-round picks you'll find for rotisserie formats. Improving patience over the past two seasons also helps his points-league value, where he's worth a look, albeit one or two rounds later.

A shining star at one of the game's thinner positions, Marte has hit at least 25 home runs with an .800 OPS in each of the last three seasons. No other second baseman can claim more than one year of either number. Marte has done it with a combination of elite plate discipline, raw power and contact. In 2025, he put forth his best season from the left side of the plate (.288/.377/.519 rates) since 2019, addressing one of the few previously ordinary facets of his game. The only knocks on Marte now are questions about an eventual career downslope, as he'll play 2026 at age 32, and his injury history, as he has missed at least 25 games in four of the past five seasons. They're minor questions, however, and drafting him as a foundational part of your fantasy team should pay big dividends from a tough-to-fill lineup spot.

After a massive rookie breakthrough in middle relief in 2024, Smith graduated to closer status last August, going 13-for-16 converting his saves with a 2.60 ERA and 39 K's compared to two walks over the season's final two months. Considering he was fantasy baseball's top point scorer among relievers during that time (162 points), there's every reason to believe he can contend for that status working in the role full-time in 2026. Smith has been especially dominant against left-handed hitters (.162/.218/.270 rates in his two MLB seasons), and he made big strides in minimizing hard contact last year -- a combination that makes him one of the safest investments at his position despite his limited closer experience.

Between his having bulked up, made a batting-stance adjustment and adopted a torpedo bat during the prior winter, Rice's breakthrough last season had plenty of rationale. His hard-hit rate spiked by 20%, and he finished sixth among batting title-eligible hitters in expected wOBA. But perhaps most important for fantasy purposes, Rice put in enough time the plate to qualify at catcher, where his offensive contributions carry far more weight than at first base. Rice could again split time between the two positions, but consider that his 26 homers last season ranked fifth among catcher-eligibles for 2026. He's an up-and-comer well worth an early-round pick.

The fireballer put together his best season ever at age 37, successfully converting 32 of 34 save chances for the Red Sox during the regular season with a career-low 1.17 ERA. Chapman was virtually untouchable in the ninth inning with his trademark fastball and nasty breaking pitch. Shockingly, he cut his walk rate down to a career-low mark of 6.6 percent after being at or above 15 percent each of the prior four seasons. It was the dramatic reversal in that particular department that fueled his renaissance, though it's understandable to be skeptical given his history of control woes. Signed to an extension last August, Chapman will return to the closer role to which he is highly accustomed and attempt to continue bucking historical trends with his dominance at an advanced age.

Known as a great player with a spotty health history, Seager fell short of 125 games played for the third consecutive regular season, landing at just 102 games with the Rangers in 2025. The shortstop made multiple trips to the injured list early with a hamstring strain and missed the final month following an appendectomy. Even so, he reached 20 homers for the fourth consecutive campaign and for the sixth time in his career, having smacked 30-plus each of the three seasons prior to last. Seager has lost a bit off his batting average in recent years, as his numbers against lefties are in decline, but he still crushes right-handed pitching when available. Steals are not part of the equation and players don't typically get healthier in their 30s, but the five-time All-Star still offers a high upside if he can somehow stay on the field.

The Cubs entered the season with an organizational focus on pulling more flyballs, and Suzuki set the tone by increasing his pull rate while maintaining an above-average flyball rate. The approach yielded new career highs with the Cubs in ISO and home runs. That power jump came with a 38-point drop in batting average, though his xBA was only three points lower than the prior season. His strikeout rate ticked down slightly but remained well above league average. Most notably, Suzuki appeared in 151 games, marking his first season since coming over in which he avoided the IL entirely. Often, a year after a major adjustment is used to recalibrate, but Suzuki would be best served sticking with the same approach and hoping his batting average moves closer to his expected mark.

Springer found the Fountain of Youth in 2025 with a .309 average, 32 homers and 18 steals across 140 regular-season games. He also tied for ninth in MLB in runs scored with 106 while often setting the table for a potent Blue Jays lineup. The incredible resurgence continued into October, with Springer posting an .899 OPS and four more homers during Toronto's run to the pennant. At 35 years old, Springer spent the majority of his time at designated hitter, though he still qualifies in the outfield. Prior to last season, Springer was in steady decline, bottoming out in 2024. However, in 2025 he looked nothing at all like a player on his last gasp in the major leagues. The DH tag should in theory help preserve his health in his late-30s.

Strider's recovery from an April 2024 UCL repair -- his second such major elbow surgery -- got off to a solid start, as he had two games with double-digit strikeouts and averaged 12.3 fantasy points across his first 12 starts. Diminished fastball velocity and a ballooning walk rate would undermine him thereafter, as he had a 5.46 ERA and averaged just 4.3 fantasy points over his final 11 turns. It's difficult to pinpoint the reasons behind Strider's late struggles, with the easiest explanation being the challenging road back from UCL surgery, but his inconsistency is a concern for fantasy managers. When healthy, he has elite stuff that can make him one of the best pitchers in the game, but the risk involved makes him more of a middle-of-your-staff type come 2026 drafts.

No other active closer has more saves than Hader over the past five seasons. His 28.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage lead all closers in that time, as well. Throw in the fourth-best WHIP and the second-best batting average against, and you may ask yourself why there is any reason Hader is not the first closer off the board in fantasy drafts. The answer to that question lies in the uncertainty surrounding his health, as he came down with shoulder soreness in early August and never returned to the mound, then dealt with biceps inflammation at the onset of spring training. It is also worth remembering that Hader was coming off a post-COVID high for workload from 2024 to 2025, which could help explain the injuries. Keep tabs on his progress as Opening Day approaches.

Heralded for his defense at third base, Chapman does not hit for a high batting average (career .240) but has been above a .750 OPS in all but one of his nine big-league seasons to date. Chapman has been a consistent contributor with 20-plus homers four of the past five years, reaching 21 with the Giants last season despite multiple trips to the IL with a hand injury he first suffered while diving back into the first-base bag in June. Chapman has added steals in the years since MLB limited the number of throws to first base among other rule changes to facilitate the running game, and he's now well established as a net positive on both sides of the ball. The two-time Platinum Glover projects to continue batting fourth or fifth on a daily basis for San Francisco, health permitting.

For what seemed like the umpteenth year in a row, Snell was excellent when available to his fantasy managers � which didn't happen especially often. Among the 61 pitchers who have made at least 87 starts over the last four seasons, he ranks first in strikeout rate (31.9%), second in ERA (2.76), fifth in fantasy points per start (13.9) and seventh in hard-hit rate allowed (34.8%). The problem? That's exactly the number of starts Snell made in that time, which is under 22 per year. It's remarkable that he has been able to maintain such a high level of productivity around his many absences, but credit the Dodgers for being among the best at maximizing pitcher workloads and utility when available. We see no reason for that to change now. So, how lucky do you feel?

Glasnow was unable to repeat his overall performance from 2024 when he set a new career high with just 134 innings of work, but did at least post a career-best 3.19 ERA over the 18 starts he made. The ERA was surprising since his walk rate jumped from 6.7 percent to 11.7 percent last season, dropping his normally stellar K-BB to a career-low 17.2 percent. Glasnow was still impossible to hit as the league hit .175 against him last season, which is not surprising since only Freddy Peralta, Jacob deGrom and Max Scherzer have been tougher to hit amongst all starting pitchers in baseball since Glasnow joined the league in 2016. Glasnow has some of the nastiest stuff in baseball, but he also has one of the most fragile bodies as something always breaks down. Expect 120 innings of valuable contributions but not much more.

First, the good: On a per-start basis, Greene's skills took a noticeable step forward in 2025, as he set personal bests with his 31.4% strikeout and 6.2% walk rates, 68.8% rate of first-pitch strikes and 99.5 mph average fastball velocity. Then, the bad: He spent more than a month on the IL for the fourth consecutive season, this time missing 85 days across two stints for a groin strain. It underscores Greene's risk/reward status for fantasy leagues, as his raw stuff makes him a legitimate Cy Young contender when he's healthy --which he unfortunately hasn't been fully across any of his four MLB seasons. Considering every pitcher seems to be an injury risk these days, however, and that Greene will play 2026 at a prime-age 26, reward seems to be the smarter driving draft-day force.

Traded from Anaheim in November, Ward will be part of the new-look Orioles under new skipper Craig Albernaz in 2026. Ward's tenure with the Angels culminated in career highs in home runs (36) and RBI (103) last season, with the outfielder ranking in the top six in the AL in both categories, after previously topping out at 25 homers and 75 RBI in 2024. The right-handed slugger continues to mash lefties, and he at least hits for power against same-side arms if not for batting average. Ward added to his walk rate last season and his offensive contributions more than made up for his defensive limitations. Now 32, Ward should be in position to knock in the runners Pete Alonso leaves on base while batting in the middle of the everyday lineup in Baltimore.

Widely regarded as the top prospect in all of baseball, Griffin's skill set is regarded so highly that he has generated some chatter that he could break camp with the Pirates and perhaps even win the NL  Rookie of the Year Award, despite only one year's pro experience under his belt. What a debut year it was, as he hit 21 homers, stole 65 bases, hit .333/.415/.527, played solid shortstop and performed equally well across three competitive levels through Double-A. Griffin is the kind of future-MVP-caliber prospect that dynasty league managers should build around. Redraft managers should scoop him up instantly upon his promotion. If you've got space to stash him, a realistic ETA in Pittsburgh might be before mid-season.

Baseball's greatest historical two-way player could be primed for his best season yet. On offense in 2025, Ohtani exceeded 50 home runs for a second consecutive season and stole 20-plus bases for a third straight year. On the mound, the Dodgers were uber-conservative with his recovery from his September 2023 elbow reconstruction, but Ohtani delivered per-start numbers in line with his pre-injury rates. His pitching usage also ramped up right in time for the playoffs, during which he became the first player in history to hit three home runs while also striking out 10 batters in one game in the Dodgers' NLCS clincher, triggering memories of his 2022, when he scored 411 fantasy points as a hitter and 475 as a pitcher. As the Dodgers surely will, so must you manage his daily utility -- he can be used as a DH or pitcher, but not both --  but Ohtani's potential puts him head and shoulders ahead of the pack.

Raleigh's historic year -- he set single-season records for most home runs by a catcher (60) and drove in more runs (125) than any backstop had in 51 years -- is less subject to regression than you might think. He adopted an extremely fly ball-oriented approach at the plate, posting the highest qualified fly-ball rate in 13 years and the majors' fourth-best Barrel rate. Raleigh's raw power is as legitimate as anyone's in the game, even if it comes at the expense of many strikeouts and a low batting average. It makes him the top catcher, though his fantasy worth ultimately comes down to your league settings. In ESPN leagues, he's such a stalwart at a thin position that he's a borderline first-rounder. In deeper two-catcher leagues, Raleigh's 2025 headlines could cause him to be drafted too aggressively, ignoring the fact that 60 homers is a near impossibility to repeat.

Fresh off a career year in 2024 and with his team moving to one of baseball's most hitter-friendly environments in Sacramento last season, Rooker seemed primed to potentially take another step forward. Come year's end, his 2025 had an eerie 2023 look to it, albeit with some key improvements. He traded some of his power for contact, with his fly-ball rate plummeting by 4% but his contact rate improving by roughly the same margin. The end result probably prevents Rooker from winning future home run crowns, but for as long as he calls Sutter Health Park his home, he'll be good for at least his 2025 numbers, if not better.

For the first time since 2017, Buxton played more than two-thirds of his team's games last season, though he still made two more trips to the IL (totaling 29 days). OK, we'll still call it a win! Better health led to a complete restoration of his top-shelf raw power and speed metrics and, thanks in part to a career high in plate appearances, he managed another personal best with 35 home runs and was a perfect 24-for-24 stealing bases. Consider it a reminder of what Buxton can contribute at his best, as he's still a close-to-prime 32 years of age albeit with sterling speed metrics. His extensive injury history will -- and should --always keep your draft-day expectations in check. He's also still preferable in rotisserie than in points leagues, but his upside when healthy warrants mid-round consideration.

After missing only eight games from 2021 to 2023, Riley played just 110 in 2024 and 102 last season, dealing with a fluke broken hand two years ago and three IL visits for core issues last year. His sports hernia surgery in August should help him re-establish his reliability. Even through the injuries, Riley maintained near-elite exit velocity, barrel rate and hard-hit numbers. However, after slightly improving his strikeout rate from 2021-23, he gave back those gains last year, posting his worst rate since his rookie season. It was likely more a matter of his timing being affected by the injury-driven absences than a change in approach. The market is not quite as bullish as in prior years, but at a thin position full of uncertainty, Riley stands out as a risk worth taking.

Diaz took advantage of his home digs in 2025, hitting 18 of his career-high 25 homers at Steinbrenner Field. He was no slouch on the road with a .780 OPS, but the Rays' move back to Tropicana Field in 2026 looms large as Diaz has 37 homers in 338 career games at the Trop. While he may not have standout power, he has tapped into more in recent years, enough to supplement his high batting average and make Diaz a fantasy standout if not quite a superstar. Primarily a DH at this stage, Diaz retains first-base eligibility for at least one more season, and a case can be made that he's underrated among the wider drafting public. Expect him to continue batting in the top third of the order every single day in his age-34 season.

Baseball's top-scoring fantasy pitcher over the first four seasons of his Yankees career (2020-23), Cole missed the first three months of 2024 due to an elbow injury, then ultimately succumbed to 2025-ending Tommy John surgery last March. A 14-month recovery timetable would have him ready to rejoin the big-league club in May, though the variability of return date and initial performance level coming off that operation lends uncertainty to his 2026 draft stock. Cole will be one of the most important pitchers to track once he resumes game competition (exhibition or minor-league level) in the spring, but his skill set makes him one of the best IL stashes for prospective front-of-a-staff fantasy production in the season's second half (or even its final four months).

Gray and Lady Luck have been at odds for the last two years. In 2024, his ERA was pegged about a run too high by xFIP, and last season, his 4.28 ERA was deemed roughly a run higher than its estimators. His BABIP and HR/FB rate were elevated, while his LOB percentage was suppressed. Gray eclipsed 180 frames for the second straight season, which he had last accomplished in 2015. For the second consecutive season, his velocity slipped, but he waived his no-trade clause to join the Red Sox, who specialize in teaching pitchers to work off breaking balls and offspeed stuff, and Gray can throw multiple types. Gray's home runs have crept up over the past two seasons, and the Green Monster has a habit of turning routine flyballs into doubles, so Gray may need to get back in favor with Lady Luck. Father Time looms, but for now, Gray remains dependable.

At casual glance, Pepiot's 2025 has the guise of �spinning his wheels� or worse, a small step backwards. His ERA rose by more than a quarter of a run, he averaged 0.1 fewer fantasy points per start, and he whiffed only 24.6% of the hitters he faced after 26.3% the year before. Make no mistake, however, that the Rays' return to Tropicana Field for 2026 is a huge positive for Pepiot, who surrendered 17 homers (among 26 total) at what was the majors' seventh most-favorable home run environment in 2025. He's a capable, now built-up starting pitcher who could be ready to take another step forward into top-25 SP territory.

Murakami, who hit 223 home runs over a six-year span (2019-24) in Japan, put off a move to the States one winter ago, only to suffer an injury-plagued 2025 campaign. Between elbow surgery and a nagging oblique issue, he played only 69 games, though his power potential upon his return was as excellent as ever. He hit 24 homers, slugged .659 and had .373 isolated power for the season. The White Sox took a $34 million chance on him to play first base, which at least offers additional positional flexibility for his fantasy managers. Just 26 years old, Murakami is a �three true outcomes� style lefty slugger, which could elicit within White Sox fans memories of Adam Dunn (the Chicago version) on the high end, or Daniel Palka on the low end. Fantasy managers would be best to split the difference and draft accordingly.

Schlittler went from being a prospect afterthought entering the 2024 minor-league season to becoming the first pitcher in postseason history to pitch eight scoreless innings of at least 12 strikeouts (with zero walks) in the 2025 Wild Card Series. Such demonstrates the magnitude of his unexpected breakthrough. Thanks to his improved, 98.0-mph fastball and cutter, he scored the 19th-most fantasy points from the date of his July 9 debut forward, with stellar underlying metrics that support his ability to approach or match the effort over a full 2026. Schlittler is a strong mid-round, middle-of-your-staff pick for fantasy purposes, assuming the back issues that popped up as spring training dawned don't become a lingering issue.

The Cardinals' top prospect entering 2026, Wetherholt would make a lot of sense for them in their Opening Day lineup, considering their shift to a rebuild and February’s trade of Brendan Donovan. Wetherholt has torn through three minor-league levels in just 14 months (and 138 games), batting a robust .314/.416/.562 with 10 homers and nine steals in 47 season-concluding games for Triple-A Memphis last year. He has an elite plate approach, which should ease his transition to the majors and make him particularly attractive in points leagues. He's a dynasty building block and, if he breaks camp as the team's second baseman or shortstop as expected, would be a top Rookie of the Year candidate.

Bradish underwent Tommy John surgery with an internal brace in June 2024 but returned to start six games down the stretch. While command and control can lag after surgery, he showed little rust, striking out 47 batters against just 10 walks over 32 innings, with velocity in line with his healthy years. The performance was encouraging, but he has totaled only 104.2 innings across the majors and minors over the past two seasons. That likely points to workload management ahead, and expecting him to sustain last season's pace, even if it mirrors his healthy 2023, may be optimistic. A cautious approach is warranted.

After four straight seasons of above-average production, Reynolds slipped to slightly below the norm, driven by a spike in his strikeout rate and a BABIP that didn't align with his batted-ball mix. He failed to gain the typical batting average boost that comes with more groundballs and line drives. His batting average dropped 30 points from the prior season, while his slugging finished 45 points below 2024. That said, his xBA was actually one point higher, and his xSLG was only 25 points short of the previous year. The downturn extended to the running game, as Reynolds went just 3-for-5 in steal attempts after going a combined 22-for-25 over the prior two seasons. Just 31 years old, Reynolds appears capable of a rebound if his strikeout and flyball rates move back toward earlier levels.

One of 2025's most unexpected breakthrough performers, Perdomo joined Shohei Ohtani and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only players with at least a .275 batting average, 20 home runs, 20 stolen bases and a 7.0 WAR. Everything clicked for Perdomo, from the counting numbers-inflating 129 starts he made out of the top three spots in the lineup, to the 8.4% HR/FB rate that was more than double his MLB career number entering the year, though those are two areas now subject to some regression. His contact-skills growth represented the bigger story, elevating his floor and making him an ideal points-league pick. So long as you're not expecting a repeat of his 20 homers or 100 RBI, he should be a fine early-to-mid-round pick.

The Athletics traded Erceg to the Royals at the 2024 trade deadline, and after notching holds in his first five outings, he was installed as the closer. However, Kansas City signed Carlos Estevez in the offseason, relegating Erceg to setup duties last season. He delivered 23 holds and chipped in with a pair of saves and eight wins, but there was a noticeable change under the hood, as Erceg's strikeout rate plummeted nine points. His ERA was unaffected by the decline, as he posted a career-low mark, though estimators pegged it as more than a run too low. His velocity dropped a tick across the board, likely contributing to the strikeout dip. Erceg's season ended in mid-September with a shoulder impingement, but he's expected to be ready for camp. Monitor his velocity; without a rebound, he's risky as a reliable source of holds.

Alvarez's 2025 was an injury nightmare, from the hand injury he suffered in April -- initially diagnosed as a sprain but ultimately discovered to be a small fracture -- to the season-ending ankle sprain he suffered in September, just 19 games into his return from the prior ailment. It unfortunately continued a pattern of health questions for the Astros slugger who, when healthy, has consistently proven himself to be one of the best all-around hitters in the game. From 2021-24, Alvarez ranked third in OPS (.946) and hard-hit rate (53.8%) and seventh in batting average (.294). Bear in mind that during those 19 late-season, healthy games, he posted significantly better numbers in all three of those categories. A healthy spring training would go a long way towards easing prospective fantasy managers' nerves with this extreme risk/reward pick, but he's far too talented to let slip much further than the first 20 or so picks of any draft.

When a 131 wRC+ is your lowest mark since 2019, the bar is clearly high. It is fair to attribute Harper's dip to first-half elbow and wrist issues, the latter requiring a three-plus-week IL stint. However, a look under the hood reveals a low BABIP on outfield line drives that masked Harper's otherwise strong performance. His barrel, hard-hit and strikeout rates were consistent with prior seasons, but unfavorable batted-ball outcomes drove the drop in production. The good news is that a low outfield line-drive BABIP is not a sign of skills deterioration, just poor luck. Still, Harper missed 30 games, continuing a five-year pattern of IL visits. He remains a five-category contributor when healthy, as shown by 12 stolen bases in 14 attempts last season, though durability remains a concern. Harper is no longer a fantasy building block, but his draft stock remains high, as fear of missing out is a strong bias.

Through four months of 2025, Crow-Armstrong seemed on track for top-level MVP votes, in rotisserie terms providing more earnings than any player other than Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani. Regression and his own free-swinging nature at the plate hit Crow-Armstrong hard over the final two months, however, as he hit just .188/.237/.295 and struck out in more than 25% of his trips to the plate. In his defense, Crow-Armstrong's elite speed gives him a steady valuation base in rotisserie leagues, and his Platinum Glove-caliber defense assures him of regular playing time -- which helps boost his points-league value. Improved patience would be his ticket to stardom in the latter, but in the former, he's already a building-block draft pick.

Wood got off to a torrid start to his first full MLB season, batting .278/.381/.534 with 24 homers in 95 first-half games to earn himself an All-Star appearance. The holes in his ground ball-oriented swing, however, caught up with him thereafter, and he hit just .223/.301/.388 with an MLB-leading 105 strikeouts the rest of the way. Wood will need to address those shortcomings, or add some loft to his swing, in order to develop into a true offensive superstar, but few players have the kind of top-shelf metrics in terms of bat speed and contact quality. He's a player to watch during March to see what kinds of adjustments he makes, though as is he's a high-ceiling, early-to-mid-round selection with more upside in rotisserie than points leagues.

A rotator cuff strain cost Ragans three months of 2025, entirely thwarting his rise to becoming one of fantasy baseball's premier starters. That, coupled with a groin strain that cost him 19 days in May/June, cast him as somewhat of an injury risk entering 2026, but be aware that these ailments did little to diminish his excellent skill set. Ragans' final two regular-season starts (among the three he made in September) had him striking out 18 out of 35 batters, with similar levels of velocity and swing-and-miss rates to those pre-injury. He'll need careful examination during spring training for any lingering health issues, but a dominant Ragans in March could help make a case for him to be a top-10 fantasy starter come draft day.

In his seventh season in the majors, Luzardo finally parlayed his high-90s fastball and whiff-generating sweeper and changeup into the breakthrough year fantasy managers had long anticipated. In fact, if not for back-to-back starts early in the season in which he surrendered a combined 20 earned runs, he might have garnered Cy Young votes and been a more prominent name heading into 2026 drafts. No matter, as that might make Luzardo a potential fantasy ace at the price of a mid-staff starter. He's no longer quite the injury risk he once was, with a pair of 32-start seasons in the past three years and, while he calls one of the more hitter-friendly environments his home, he gets some of the best lineup and bullpen support of any pitcher in the league.

If you believe in such folly, it's an even-numbered year, so based upon past patterns, Cease is destined for greatness in 2026. He's a modern-day Bret Saberhagen, but with strikeouts! Cease's FIP tells a more rational tale, as he has fluctuated by less than two-thirds of a run in the category over the past five seasons, a signal that luck factors have been friendly to him in those even-numbered campaigns, but harsh in odd years. What fuels bounce-back chatter with Cease isn't the date on the calendar, but rather his new team's defense, as the Blue Jays are significantly better in the field than were the 2025 Padres. See, luck can be controlled � somewhat, at least. Don't let Cease slip beyond the first few rounds of your draft.

Greene took his career to another level in 2025, setting career highs in all run production categories, but with a strikeout rate of 30.7 percent. The young outfielder was an everyday player for Detroit because he was so good despite the fact his output against lefties remains a problem. Ten of Greene's 60 homers over the past two seasons have come off lefties, while he has been limited to a .216 average against southpaws. Meanwhile, along with the 50 homers against righties, Greene has a .278/.349./532 slash line versus them. His below-league-average strikeout rate from 2024 rose last season, which ultimately holds back how hopeful anyone can realistically be about BA improvement. The strikeout rate is the same against both righties and lefties. He's a four-category producer at risk of dropping to three if he can't curb the growing swing-and-miss in his stroke.

A hot start to Cruz's 2025 -- he had eight homers and 14 stolen bases through his first 30 games -- seemed to signal the arrival of his long-anticipated breakthrough. However, over time, his former weaknesses continued to squeak through. He posted the third-worst contact rate (66.0%) and 16th-lowest launch angle (8.1 degrees) among batting title-eligibles, capping his power upside. He also hit an abysmal .102/.224/.176 against lefties, rendering him more of a matchups type. Now 27, Cruz still has time to patch those flaws in his game, but he's shaping up as more of a rotisserie-minded breakthrough candidate than a complete, all-around star. Think carefully before reaching for him in points-league drafts.

Bednar's overall 2025 numbers were so good that you almost forget he was sent to Triple-A early in the season because he got off to such an awful start. Bednar had a rough spring and then blew two of his first three save chances opening weekend with some bad command and worse batted-ball luck which led Pittsburgh to send him to Indianapolis for some fine-tuning. Bednar returned three weeks later and was utterly dominant as a closer, winning six games and saving 26 more while striking out 83 batters and limited opposing hitters to a .183 average in his time between the Pirates and Yankees. Whereas he was a fringe top closer option heading into 2025, he is now a firm first-closer option in 2026 with the Yankees fully confident in Bednar's abilities as evidenced by them letting Devin Williams and Luke Weaver depart in free agency.

One of 2025's biggest disappointments, Williams simply couldn't get the job done in the ninth for the Yankees. It took him just one month to get removed as their closer, after he surrendered as many earned runs in that time (10) as he had during the entirety of his career-year 2023. His season-ending ERA wound up being nearly three full runs higher than the total over his first six MLB seasons. In Williams' strong defense, however, he had outrageous numbers over the final four months in terms of batting average allowed (.172) and strikeout rate (38.6%) -- and he was done in by a 55.2 LOB% that was lower than any qualified reliever had posted in three years. The Mets, who signed him to serve as their 2026 closer, surely saw this and expect a full rebound. We tend to agree.

Wheeler was amid one of the most remarkable five-year runs of any active pitcher at the time he succumbed to thoracic outlet surgery last September. Even missing the season's final six weeks, from 2021-25, he ranked first among pitchers in fantasy points (2,327), first in WHIP (1.00), tied for first in quality starts (99), second in strikeouts (1,041), third in ERA (2.90), tied for third in wins (65), fourth in innings pitched (908) and fifth in K/BB ratio (5.10). Wheeler's recovery timetable should place a return sometime around May 1, though there are risks involved with the speed and effectiveness of pitchers' rehabilitation, and his advancing age (35) raises an additional concern. He showed no ill effects of the aging process before the operation, however, so if you're willing to stash him in an IL spot hoping he makes a swift recovery, he still has an ace's fantasy ceiling.

Suarez's "HR or nothing" approach at the plate paid its biggest dividends in 2025, from his four-homer game in late April, to his season-ending career bests of 49 HR, 118 RBI, 40.9% fly ball and 47.6% hard-hit rates. Shifting his swing in that direction over the years has put him at an elevated risk of low batting averages, however, as well as peaks and valleys in his performance. That's not the kind of profile that seems likely to age well, and Suarez will play most of 2026 at 34 years of age. Expect some regression in the power department, though he should still put the ball over the fence frequently enough to remain a top-10 fantasy third baseman.

Despite Woodruff recently missing the better part of two years and ending 2025 back on the injured list with a lat strain, Milwaukee extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which speaks to just how well he pitched when available last season. After his recovery from 2023 shoulder surgery was set back several times, Woodruff finally returned with five quality starts in his first six outings before enduring a couple hiccups in August. His xBA and xERA were both among the very best in baseball in his limited sample of 64.2 big-league innings last season. The right-hander has always gotten whiffs and the Brewers have proven they know what they're doing in regards to pitching. Chasing a full season's worth of starts would be a fool's errand, but the team clearly has high hopes for Woodruff in regards to both performance and workload.

Shaky control and a knee injury sustained during a game of Hacky Sack ruined Uribe's 2024, which began with the promise of potential save chances (including in four of the team's first six games). He'd settle for a middle relief role to begin 2025, from which he was every bit as excellent as he was across the final three months of his 2023 debut campaign. Uribe led the league in holds (37) and was third among relievers in both ERA and hard-hit rate allowed. Plus, he managed six saves and a 1.89 ERA in 18 games between the regular season and postseason after stepping back into the closer role for an injured Trevor Megill. That breakthrough puts Uribe in direct competition with Megill for the team's ninth-inning role this season, with your league's inclusion of saves or holds ultimately determining Uribe's value. He'll be one of the best closers or holds-getters, however it shakes out.

Musgrove missed all of last season while rehabbing from the Tommy John surgery he underwent in October 2024, but he should be good to go for the start of 2026 given that he was throwing multi-inning bullpen sessions late last season. The veteran right-hander has a 3.25 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 9.6 K/9 since the start of the 2020 campaign, but there are major question marks regarding his durability as he enters his age-33 season. Musgrove made just 36 starts across 2023 and 2024 due to injuries (even before the Tommy John injury), and he's now coming off a lost season and major elbow surgery. Regaining his strong form in the first year back wouldn't be unheard of, but Musgrove's additional injury issues add another layer to consider. His ceiling is that of a top-end starter, but the floor here is zero.

McGonigle hit .305/.408/.583 in 88 games across three minor-league levels last season, walking 13 more times than he struck out, while hitting 19 homers and stealing 10 bases. He's perhaps the most well-rounded prospect among those with a likely 2026 ETA, and the Tigers have the option of breaking him in at either second base or shortstop once he's ready. McGonigle's skill set is great for all fantasy play, but he's looking like a prospective points-league gem. Consider him a dynasty building block and a �must get� in redrafts the moment he's promoted.

Bradley had an underwhelming 4.61 ERA in 21 starts for Tampa Bay in 2025 before being traded to Minnesota, where he struggled even more with a 6.61 ERA in six outings. He posted a career-worst 8.0 K/9 and 3.5 BB/9 last season but also had a career-best 1.2 HR/9. Bradley has shown flashes of brilliance since making his MLB debut in 2023 but has been mostly ineffective, with the drop in strikeouts negating the one area in which he still provided fantasy value. Bradley isn't guaranteed to begin 2026 with a spot in Minnesota's rotation, but the Twins seem likely to give him a chance to get back on track in the big leagues given how hard they committed to selling at the trade deadline last summer.

After years of outperforming his expected ERA, Gallen didn't get much favor from Lady Luck in 2025. He had the eighth-widest ERA-xERA differential among qualifiers, he posted a career-worst 21.5% strikeout rate and he had an ERA over 4.00 in five out of six months. Still, Gallen continued to pitch effectively enough deep into games, his 33 starts being second-most and 192 innings eighth-most in the league. Plus, he had a 3.32 ERA over his final 11 starts. Back with the Diamondbacks after a long winter on the free-agent market, Gallen is a strong points-league option as one of the more durable starters out there.

One of baseball's best bat handlers -- he's one of four players with at least 85% contact and 27.5% line-drive rates and 500 plate appearances over the last two seasons combined -- Donovan's skill set makes him one of the most underrated points-league players, even if he's only a back-of-your-roster utility type in rotisserie formats. Traded to the Mariners in February, he’ll likely serve as their leadoff man against right-handed pitchers, giving him more of a matchup lean in shallow mixed leagues but also boosting his run-scoring potential on the whole. Donovan's ceiling isn't especially high, but he's likely to deliver another top-100 fantasy point total in 2026.

An elbow issue that required offseason surgery bumped Herrera off catcher and to DH around midseason, at a point in 2025 too early for him to log the requisite time to maintain eligibility behind the plate. It's a shame, as his skill set -- solid contact, plate discipline skills and pop, as well as aggressiveness on the bases -- is intriguing for fantasy purposes from a catcher, but much more commonplace from a DH (a position that lets you use anyone). The Cardinals claim that Herrera should be able to return to catching duties in 2026, but his defensive limitations there might slow that process. Considering he'd have a top-10 ceiling at catcher, take a flier on him late and keep your fingers crossed.

Weathers didn't make his season debut in 2025 until mid-May due to a forearm strain, and he landed back on the injured not long thereafter due to a lat injury. The left-hander finished the campaign with just eight starts, though he pitched well in those appearances with a 3.99 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and 37:12 K:BB over 38.1 innings. Weathers hasn't made more than 16 appearances in a season since working as a swingman as a rookie with the Padres in 2021. He has a 3.75 ERA and 1.21 WHIP across the past two seasons, but he simply hasn't been healthy enough to move the needle for fantasy managers. Weathers could factor into the Yankees' rotation for as long as he can take the mound, but he's likely to have a limited workload even if healthy given that he's yet to throw 100 frames in a season as a big leaguer.

One of baseball's most consistent, well-rounded players, Ramirez is one of only two with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of the past five seasons, averaging 31.6 and 32.0 over that time. He's also one of only four with at least a batting title-qualified 80% contact rate in all of those years. From a fantasy point-scoring perspective, he has finished top 10 among hitters in each of the past six seasons, which is twice as long as the players with the next-longest such streaks (3, by Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto). Ramirez's 33 years of age raise slight concerns that his decline phase could soon gradually begin, but for 2026, at least, his five-tool ability makes him one of the top picks in any fantasy format.

Finally beyond the injury issues that plagued him for much of his first six MLB seasons, Tatis delivered the most well rounded year of his career to date. Though he posted the lowest HR rate of his career (3.6%, resulting in a total of just 25 taters), he vastly improved his contact and his patience at the plate, setting personal bests with his 73.0% contact and 24.1% chase rates. The result was more fantasy points (439) than Tatis scored in 2021 (422), when he hit 42 home runs, and it sets him up for potentially greater things in 2026 as a 27-year-old. He's not without injury risk based upon his track record, but with his skills now making him nearly as strong a pick in points-based as rotisserie leagues, he's a legitimate building block player for fantasy purposes.

Tucker's cumulative 2025 numbers don't remotely do justice to his immense raw talent. Breaking it down by halves, he hit .291/.395/.537 with 17 homers and 20 steals through the season's first three months, which is top 10 in fantasy valuation in both points-based and rotisserie scoring. He then cratered to .225/.348/.342 rates with just five homers and five steals over the final three months, placing outside the top 190 players overall. Following the season, Tucker revealed that he had been playing through a hand fracture suffered in early June, an explanation that affords promise of a complete rebound from him following the winter's rest. The Dodgers are clearly banking on that, granting him the second-highest contract average annual value of any player in history, while placing him in the heart of a loaded lineup. Anticipate Tucker bouncing back and consider him a first rounder still.

People might call him Mr. Smile, but around these parts, we like to call him Mr. Consistency. Lindor has averaged 32 home runs and 30 stolen bases for the past three seasons and, had he stolen one more base in 2024, he'd have joined Barry Bonds (1995-97) as the only players to go 30/30 in three straight years. Lindor's underlying metrics took a slight step backwards last season, hardly shocking from a then-31-year-old, but that's countered by his being one of the game's most durable players, averaging 158 games the past four seasons. If there's any knock on him, it's that he has a history of somewhat slow starts, his first-half career OPS being 57 points lower than in the second half. Lindor is also questionable for Opening Day following hamate bone surgery in February, which could also extend his tendency for sluggish Aprils. No matter, as if his top-20 overall draft stock isn't to your liking (but it should be!), simply jot down his drafting manager's cell phone number and remember to make a trade-inquiry call around May 15.

Devers has been a star since he hit the scene in 2017, but 2025 saw him come to a career crossroads due to an unwillingness to make a much-needed defensive change which ultimately led to him being traded from Boston midseason. The turmoil began in camp and carried over to the regular season when Devers began the season 2-for-27 with 15 strikeouts. He recovered nicely and went onto hit .289/.416/.528 before the infighting became too much and he was sent to San Francisco. The move to Oracle Park and the National League had an impact on his numbers as he hit .236/.347/.480 the rest of the season, but with 20 of his 35 homers after the trade. By season's end, the counting category production was where it should have been even as his average suffered. The now 1B/DH is still an early-round selection.

Last season was a career year for Langeliers, and there were two specific things which held him back from getting even more attention: an oblique injury which cost him some time in the summer, and Cal Raleigh stealing all the spotlight. Langeliers was on a 40-homer pace, and while many will credit the comforts of Sutter Health Park in Sacramento, that would be a mistake as Langeliers hit 19 of his 31 home runs on the road. He increased his power output while also cutting down his strikeout rate from the previous season. The club went as far as to use Brent Rooker in the field despite his defensive limitations to allow Langeliers some half-days off at DH. Langeliers' draft stock has improved as much as any player in baseball, and with all arrows pointing in the right direction, he should be one of the top fantasy catchers in MLB in 2026.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2024 Draft, Burns soared to the majors after only 13 minor-league starts, then used his 98.7-mph fastball and filthy slider to post four games of double-digit strikeouts in his first eight, as well as a 37.7% K rate over that time. While he had some issues with lefties and missed time due to a flexor strain, he did return to make five solid relief appearances and figures to make the Reds' rotation out of spring training. Burns has some work to do on improving a pitch to use against lefties, and he's a little too fly ball-oriented to avoid issues with homers in Great American Ball Park, but he's one of the most intriguing breakthrough candidates among pitchers. He's a dynasty league building block and a mid-round target in redraft formats.

Schwellenbach was well on his way towards earning Cy Young votes when a small fracture in his right elbow brought his 2025 to an abrupt stop in June. Between the final three months of 2024 and the first three of last season, he scored the fifth-most fantasy points among pitchers (502), thanks in part to a high-90s fastball and an elite, whiff-generating splitter. Unfortunately, Schwellenbach's elbow issues persisted through the winter, and he required Feb. 18 surgery to remove loose bodies from his elbow. The Braves placed him on the 60-day IL at the onset of spring training, so he'll miss at least the first two months of 2026 and perhaps more than that. Schwellenbach has the upside to be a top-20 option at his position when healthy, but he's as risky a pick as they come if you're aiming to stash him for the second half.

Although a back issue cost him the first month-plus of 2025, Suarez swiftly recaptured his prior form as one of the game's best command artists, as for the fifth consecutive season he placed in at least the 70th percentile in terms of average exit velocity and hard-hit rate allowed. In fact, he tied for the season's longest consecutive quality start streak (10, May 10-June 29). These things appealed to the Red Sox, who, despite an overstuffed rotation, brought him on as a reliable, middle-of-the-staff innings eater. Fantasy managers should regard him the same way, understanding that such pitchers typically carry a little more value in points than rotisserie leagues.

After moving to a full-time starting role in 2023, Lugo survived with modest strikeout rates by limiting walks and suppressing home runs, helped by pitcher-friendly parks in Petco Park and Kauffman Stadium. He reached last season's break with a 2.67 ERA and 1.08 WHIP, seemingly following the same script, but a 4.17 xFIP hinted at looming issues. Elevated walk and home-run rates were hidden by an 87.9 percent left-on-base mark, and the correction came quickly. Over his final seven starts, Lugo posted an 8.35 ERA and 2.01 WHIP as his command and control unraveled, potentially tied to a back injury that ended his season early. On top of the strikeouts being a weak point, the late-season breakdown leaves added questions going forward.

Webb has logged the most innings of any pitcher over the past five seasons, throwing 40 more innings than any other pitcher. Over those 968.1 innings, he has logged a 3.19 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and an 18 K-BB percentage. He took his production up a level in 2025 striking out 224 batters, besting his previous career high by 30, and he did so in fewer innings than he he needed to set that previous personal record. Webb was once primarily a sinker-slider-changeup pitcher, but has also recently introduced a cutter and four-seamer to his repertoire and now both lefties and righties have to discern between five different offerings.  He is one of five pitchers to win at least 10 games in each of the past five seasons and there is little reason to think he will fall short of hitting his usual benchmarks in 2026.

Although his .224/.352/.393, 8-HR stat line through the first 55 games of 2025 gave the guise of a $765 million contract hangover, Soto's first season with the Mets, on the whole, was anything but. Over the next four months and change, he was fantasy baseball's highest-scoring player (411 points), finishing the year with a career-best 43 home runs while delivering his third consecutive season with at least 100 RBI, 125 walks and a .900 OPS. In an unusual twist, Soto also stole 38 bases, more than he had in the previous four years combined, as he went on an unreal run (pardon the pun) over the season's final two months, seemingly in a quest to join the 40/40 club. That is the facet of his game where regression seems likeliest to strike in 2026, but Soto, still a prime-age 27, remains one of the best players to build around in points leagues and a first-round pick in rotisserie formats.

Lopez was mostly a high-average speed threat for the Marlins in 2024, but he added a bit more pop in 2025 at the expense of his batting average. He batted .246 in 143 games last season -- down from .270 -- and totaled 15 home runs and 15 steals, compared to six homers and 20 stolen bases over 161 fewer plate appearances in 2024. The improved power may not stick around since Lopez still didn't consistently make hard contact, but double-digit homers with 20-plus steals is a realistic expectation at this point, though the other counting stats are likely to be limited. Lopez opened 2025 as Miami's primary second baseman but was shifted to shortstop midseason, and his strong defense at both positions will help to keep him in the lineup.

One of baseball's best power sources, Schwarber joins Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani as the only hitters with at least 180 home runs and 400 each of runs and RBI over the past four seasons, and his 18.3% Statcast Barrel rate in that time is fourth-best among qualifiers. Schwarber's keen eye at the plate, too, is an asset in points leagues, as his 426 total walks and 15.2% walk rate over that same span rank third and fourth. That he has also improved substantially against left-handed pitchers, posting his two best single-year OPS against them in the past two years, only helps cement his case as a foundational fantasy pick, even as a 33-year-old who can be slotted only at DH (UT).

Handed the Brewers' closer role at the onset of last season following the trade of Devin Williams, Megill upped both his fastball velocity and strikeout rate to score the eighth-most fantasy points among relief pitchers through late August, when he was lost for a month due to a flexor strain. Megill would return in time for the Brewers' playoff run, although Abner Uribe's performance in the interim thrusts the position into somewhat of a spring competition entering 2026. Megill figures to be the favorite to close, with similar top-10 positional production after his back-to-back elite campaigns, though this is a situation to watch throughout March.

A ruptured quadriceps tendon prematurely ended what was an otherwise excellent year for Adam in setup relief, as he turned in a second straight year of a sub-2.00 ERA and at least 25 holds and 70 strikeouts in 2025. Keep tabs on his health once spring training opens. When healthy, he’ll almost assuredly serve as Mason Miller’s primary setup man and fantasy insurance policy. Adam’s skill set is top-20 caliber among relief pitchers, so expect a return to that form sometime before midseason at the latest.

Given a chance to play daily for the first time, Caminero broke through in a big way in 2025, his 45 home runs tied for the fourth most in history by a player 22 or younger. It wasn't entirely fueled by the team's one-year stint at hitter-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, either, as Caminero hit more homers on the road (23) than at home (22), though the venue indeed benefited him as a hitter, his OPS 211 points higher in his home games. The move back to pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field for 2026 will raise some alarm bells for Caminero's prospective fantasy managers, but he has some of the best bat speed in baseball and enough contact ability to maintain a high level of impact, regardless of venue. He also finished the year on a high note, batting .291/.353/.615 with 17 homers over his final 47 games, 30 of which were played on the road. Caminero is a franchise building block for fantasy purposes.

The epitome of a risk/reward player in fantasy baseball, Acuna's career has been highlighted by extreme highs, like his historic 42/75 campaign of 2023, and painful (literally) lows, such as the separate ACL surgeries he has had on each knee in 2021 (right) and 2024 (left). It makes him one tough cookie as far as estimating his draft stock, as he has missed more games over the past five seasons (305) than any player with even a prayer of going among the top-25 picks of any mixed-league draft. However, in Acuna's defense, he has made strides in improving his plate discipline, boosting his fantasy points league stock, over the past three seasons. His contact-quality metrics last year were outstanding and he should be more willing to be aggressive on the basepaths this season as he gets further removed from his most recent ACL operation. Predicting historical outcomes is fantasy folly, but in his age-28 season, Acuna might yet roar back with another stat line for the ages.

In two seasons since shifting from relief to the rotation, Crochet has handled the move with aplomb. His 2025 reflected significant gains, not only in the 59 1/3 additional innings he tallied, but also the near-run he shaved off his ERA as well as his doubling his number of quality starts (22) relative to 2024. Crochet also gained velocity over the course of the summer, a signal that he has now settled into his role as a staff ace. He was a model of consistency, the only pitcher to score as many as 73 fantasy points in each of the season's six months. He's an ideal pitcher around whom to build your team, and a first-round pick in points leagues.

Contreras' fantasy production took a downturn in 2025, but it wasn't without explanation, as it was revealed in May that he was playing through a finger fracture dating back to the prior season -- one he endured for the near-entirety of last year. Despite that, his bat warmed along with the summer months, as a .286/.359/.465, 11-HR performance across his final 69 games offers hope that a rebound might be coming, especially after a winter of rest. Now 28, Contreras offers levels of patience and pop that few catchers can, and his 379 combined plate appearances (19% of his total) at DH over the past three seasons give him a rare volume advantage at the position. Continue to regard him one of the premier backstops.

After months of rumors, Peralta was traded from the Brewers to the Mets in January as he enters his final season before free agency. The right-hander put together a career year in 2025, leading the National League in wins with 17 to go along with a career-low 2.70 ERA across 33 starts for Milwaukee. Peralta has now reached the vaunted 30-start and 200-strikeout thresholds each of the last three years, cementing his status as a legitimate frontline starter in MLB, with three excellent secondary pitches making up for a mediocre fastball. It's entirely possible that 2025 will end up being the zenith of his career, as everything went right for him during the regular season. Regression should be built into the draft price, but the skills and track record at 29 years old make Peralta worthy of a significant investment.

Among the most shocking outcomes in fantasy baseball history has to be Naylor's 30 stolen bases last season, in a year where his Statcast sprint speed placed in the 3rd percentile -- third!!! Kudos to a guy who has one of the better success rates among base stealers historically, and is never afraid to run, but his 19 steals across 54 games once he was traded to Dan Wilson's Mariners is simply unsustainable (even though Wilson is one of the game's most aggressive managers on that front). And all this overshadows what are pretty good hitting metrics and balanced platoon splits, meaning Naylor is in about as good a place for a 20/20 potential season as he could ask. He's an underrated, early-round potential pick in rotisserie leagues, and is an early-to-mid rounder in points leagues.

The only player in history with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of his first five full MLB seasons, Arozarena joins Jose Ramirez as the only players at any point of their career to do that in each of the past five years. That provides Arozarena a strong, top-50 overall base for rotisserie fantasy play, even with his speed metrics declining slightly and this being his age-31 season. He'd need to continue improving his selectivity at the plate, however, to warrant consideration that soon in points leagues, where he's more of a mid-round selection in ESPN formats.

After eight mediocre seasons between Philadelphia and Boston, Pivetta broke out in his first year with San Diego in 2025, going 13-5 with a 2.87 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across a career-high 181.2 innings during the regular season. Not only had Pivetta never posted an ERA under 3.00 prior to last year, he hadn't posted a mark under 4.00. A flyball pitcher, Pivetta has often struggled with homers, but he cut his home-run rate way down and was especially stingy with the long ball at home in Petco Park. Although he hadn't enjoyed a high level of success prior to 2025, Pivetta often tantalized with his strikeout rates. The late bloomer will continue to take the ball every fifth day for the Padres, and expectations should be heightened but realistic.

Altuve posted a 113 wRC+, his lowest mark in a full season since 2013. While his home-run output climbed to its highest level since 2022, his batting average dipped to a career low outside of the abbreviated 2020 season. A decade ago, that might have been written off as variance, but entering his age-36 season, it may instead point toward the early stages of decline. If that is the case, erosion can accelerate quickly, introducing more risk into a profile that has been remarkably stable for years. Altuve compensated for a modest drop in barrel rate by pulling more flyballs, though there is no guarantee that adjustment sticks. With age, the downside scenarios begin to outweigh the upside, but that reality is typically reflected in the draft cost, and his dual eligibility at second base and outfield still provides some appeal.

Misiorowski, one of the game's top prospects, arrived in the majors last June to pitch five no-hit innings in his first career start, and post a 2.81 ERA and 33.7% strikeout rate across his first five. Unfortunately, between his mediocre control and the shin contusion that cost him a 17-day stay on the IL, he couldn't maintain that pace the rest of the way and his ERA ballooned to 5.36 across his final nine starts and one relief appearance. Misiorowski's raw stuff, however, was consistently excellent, and if the Brewers trust him to pitch deeper into games, he could break out in a big way in 2026. There's danger here of overrating him, but among mid-round picks, he carries a lot of upside.

A plenty-productive fantasy closer for the Cardinals over the majority of the past two seasons -- his 610 points scored from the beginning of 2024 until his 2025 deadline trade were third-most among relief pitchers -- Helsley's numbers went right into the tank following his move into setup relief for the Mets. His prior control issues and difficulty minimizing hard contact came back to haunt him, as he had a 7.20 ERA in 22 games for his new team. Undeterred by this, the Orioles signed Helsley to a two-year deal to serve as their fill-in closer, a role from which his elite velocity and past experience should make him one of the better mid-round picks at the position.

Reliever ERAs can be deceptive, and Hoffman was a clear example of that for several years. He beat his estimators in four straight seasons, running an ERA well below what his peripherals suggested. It led to expectations of regression, and his 4.37 ERA last year was his highest since 2021. Even so, a 3.21 SIERA suggests the results were inflated. While there was some skills slippage, potentially tied to a move into the AL East, the biggest problem was a sharp spike in home runs, as his 1.99 HR/9 ranked among the league's worst. Hoffman still recorded a career-high 33 saves, fourth most in baseball, but frequent long balls are a quick way to lose managerial trust, particularly in high-leverage spots like the postseason. He remains part of Toronto's saves picture, but opportunities will have to be earned, and limiting home runs will be critical.

Eovaldi threw a shutout in his second start of 2025 and pitched like a Cy Young candidate with a 1.73 ERA and 0.85 WHIP over 22 total starts for the Rangers before a rotator cuff strain ended his season in late August. The right-hander then underwent sports hernia surgery in October. While ostensibly healthy heading into 2026, Eovaldi should be considered a long shot to make 30 starts, something he's done only once over the last decade. Regression to his numbers seems inevitable, though tangible improvement can be found behind his success last season, as he dialed back his fastball usage in strategic fashion while trimming his walk rate back to elite territory. As he enters his age-36 season, the wheels are in danger of falling off, but Eovaldi is a legitimate ace when healthy.

Injuries derailed King's 2025, from the shoulder inflammation that cost him nine weeks around midseason, to the left knee inflammation that cost him one month just one start into his return from the former ailment. His raw stuff suffered accordingly (and predictably), though the winter's rest and a strong Cactus League showing could restore his potential as one of the position's top 20. When at his best, King has four offerings that generate at least a 25% whiff rate (four-seamer, changeup, sweeper and slider), and he's one of the better pitchers at suppressing hard contact. Let his March drive your draft decision, but he's at least a worthwhile risk/reward middle rounder.

For only the second time in his nine MLB seasons, Pagan seized hold of a closer opportunity and thrived in it, this time setting personal bests with his 56 games finished, 32 saves and 340 fantasy points (eight more than in his other closer year of 2019). A much-improved splitter had a lot to do with it, fueling career bests of a .161 BAA and .507 OPS allowed to lefties. That should ensure Pagan a long ninth-inning leash, though he's one of the greater risk/reward closers based upon his skill set, as an extreme fly baller whose control is only so-so. Draft Pagan in the middle rounds, once the higher-ceiling closers are gone.

Early in 2025, it again looked as though Harris's production would fall short of his skills and athleticism. He went into the All-Star break hitting .210/.234/.317, but then returned with an open stance and higher hand position and posted a .299/.315/.530 line the rest of the season. The changes more than doubled his barrel rate and lifted his hard-hit rate by nine points, placing him among the league's best in the second half. He cooled off in September, but the quality of his contact matched July and earlier levels, with August marking his best month by hard-hit rate. While his month-to-month splits raise questions about the true effect of the adjustments, the second-half surge has turned mounting frustration into tempered optimism.

Kurtz ascended to the majors just one month into the 2025 season, ready to deliver one of the most impressive power displays we've ever seen from a rookie. His 36 home runs were 10th-most in history by a rookie, his 173 OPS+ was second-best in the modern era (minimum 450 plate appearances) and his .329 isolated power was second to only Aaron Judge's .343 in 2017. In fact, Kurtz and Judge are the only players in the 11 Statcast seasons to register at least 15% Barrel and 50% hard-hit rates as rookies (again, 450-PA minimum). That Kurtz only improved as the season progressed eases the worry of any sophomore slump, and he'll still call HR-friendly Sutter Health Park his home in 2026. While history cautions against players repeating the kind of debut that Kurtz just had, he's one of the rare young sluggers with a chance to do it, making him a strong early-round selection.

Now, where did that come from? Montgomery arrived in Chicago in early July and quickly went on an uncharacteristic power surge. Over a 37-game span a few weeks after his recall, he hit 18 home runs, matching his entire 2024 total across 130 minor-league games. And that's not to say that he can't do it again, as he had strong underlying hard-contact metrics, but his 17.2% HR/FB rate, which was eighth-highest in the league from his debut date forward, hints that there'll be some pullback. Montgomery might need to improve his plate approach in order to take another step forward in 2026. As it is, he's a late-round pick for mixed-league play.

Soderstrom got off to a scorching start in 2025. Through three weeks, he was the MLB leader in home runs and was fourth among hitters in fantasy points. He ultimately delivered a modest breakthrough campaign, despite the arrival of eventual Rookie of the Year Nick Kurtz shifting him to left field in late April. While Soderstrom couldn’t maintain that lofty pace, he maintained solid power numbers, held his own against left-handed pitchers and had better road numbers away from hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park than at home. He’ll need to add more loft to his swing to take another big step forward from here, but as a 24-year-old in a good home environment for bats, he’s well worth a mid-to-late round fantasy pick.

Dominguez has settled in as a whiff-generating, righty-dominating, short reliever -- and one who has been popular on the midseason trade market -- making him a good pickup for the bullpen-starved White Sox. His experience could prove useful in a prospective spring closer competition with Grant Taylor and Jordan Leasure, though Dominguez would still be helpful in holds leagues if the team prefers to go with a younger option.

Torres enjoyed a resurgent campaign in his first season with Detroit, making his first All-Star team since 2019, though he regressed hard in the second half with a .659 OPS compared to an .812 OPS before the break. After the Tigers were eliminated from the postseason, Torres underwent sports hernia surgery. He was cleared for full activity in December. Despite the late slide, the Tigers extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which Torres accepted. With that, the 29-year-old will return to second base and presumably to the top third of the order after batting almost exclusively first or second under manager A.J. Hinch last season. While Torres does not pack the power or speed to be especially exciting for fantasy purposes, he does enough to be worthwhile in most formats.

Leiter's adjustment to big-league competition has been slow, but appreciate his 2025 growth for what it was. He posted a 3.28 ERA, seven quality starts and a 26.3% strikeout rate across 13 second-half starts and lowered his walk rate to 7.0% over his final nine outings. Equipped with a high-90s fastball and maturing slider and changeup, Leiter could be ready to take a big step forward in 2026. He has the top prospect pedigree, making him one of the more potentially profitable prospective late-round picks for your draft.

After a year away from the 30/30 club, �J-Rod� roared back to that status in 2025, with a campaign that showed relevant growth for points league managers. Rodriguez set a personal best with his 71.8% contact rate, which spiked to 77.4% over the final two months, during which time he hit .299. Between that and the gradual lowering of his ground ball rate from August forward, he could be primed for even bigger things -- perhaps a five-category monster year, or at least a boost in home runs -- as he enters his age-25 season. Rodriguez is a clear first-round talent in rotisserie leagues, but he's also a building-block player in points leagues.

After setting the Mets' franchise record for home runs in what was the most well-rounded season of his seven-year MLB career, Alonso exercised his opt-out clause to take his wares to Baltimore. There, he'll get to play in a Camden Yards that played much more HR-friendly last season after the team moved the left field fence back in, which presents a good match for a player who just set personal bests in Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates and average exit velocity. Now 31, Alonso has yet to show any signs of the aging curve taking hold, meaning he remains a top fantasy first baseman well worth a selection in the early-to-mid rounds.

After finishing seventh among pitchers in fantasy points over the final four months of 2024, Brown followed things up with six straight months of near-identical production (he'd finish sixth this time). A modest boost to his swinging-strike rate, while maintaining his elevated average fastball velocity, fueled a consistently excellent year, during which he never went more than three outings between quality starts. Brown appears to have leveled off, but he has done so as one of the premier talents at his position. He should be one of the first starting pitchers off your draft board in any format.

Baseball's consensus top prospect at the time of his June 2025 debut, Anthony put forth a promising, albeit far from eye-popping, three months of production before an oblique strain brought his year to a premature close. During that time, he managed the majors' second-best Statcast hard hit rate (60.4%) and eighth-best OBP (.396), though he put the ball on the ground too often (50.6% rate). The seeds are there for Anthony to swiftly develop into a fantasy superstar, though the progression is as likely to be gradual than all at once in 2026. So long as the cost doesn't require a guarantee of the latter, he's one of the best upside picks in the early-to-mid rounds of your draft.

Machado authored his seventh All-Star campaign in 2025, winning the Silver Slugger with 27 homers and 95 RBI across 159 games with the Padres during the regular season. The third baseman has fallen just shy of 30 homers the last two years, and his OPS has been under .800 three years running, showing a decreased but still highly respectable performance baseline. At 33 years old, Machado is not much of a runner -- he's grounded into a whopping 41 double plays over the past two seasons -- though he can still chip in a fair number of stolen bases thanks mostly to his veteran instincts. There is still a lot to like here, including durability at a position that sees a sudden drop-off in quality deeper in the player pool.

The aging curve has clearly affected Betts, as his 2025 season saw him post personal worsts in almost every statistical category, not the least of which were his .732 OPS, 35.8% hard-hit rate and 4.3% attempted steals rate. In his defense, however, he dealt with a stomach illness at the season's onset -- something that caused him to lose close to 20 pounds and affected his mechanics at the plate. Betts is fortunately in one of the absolute best environments for propping up counting numbers, as he's surrounded by a cavalcade of lineup all-stars, and he's a contact hitter whose floor isn't as perilous as most. Set your expectations at his three-year averages of a .284 batting average, 26 home runs, 88 RBI and 13 steals and you should be happy with him for the asking price.

A 4-for-35 showing in the postseason couldn't spoil what was an overall offensive breakout for the Brewers' second baseman. Turang went from ranking third in MLB with 50 steals in 2024 to 28th with just 24 steals last season, but he added surprising power and piled up the runs and RBI for a Milwaukee team that ranked third in scoring, with fantasy managers happily accepting the tradeoff for more well-rounded production. Overall, Turang added more than 30 points in batting average and nearly 130 points in OPS to finish neck and neck with Jazz Chisholm at second base in rotisserie leagues. He hits left-handed pitching well enough and seems to have established a new performance baseline, though the batted-ball profile portends a BA closer to .260 than .280 in 2026 and beyond.

Blame injuries, rather than the much-theorized �sophomore slump,� for what ailed Merrill in 2025. A hamstring strain in April, a concussion in June and an ankle sprain in August cost him a combined 44 games and three IL stints, between which he struggled to garner any sort of momentum. It ultimately caused him to attempt zero stolen bases after June 14. Despite this, Merrill sported similarly strong contact-quality metrics to those of his rookie 2024, and he finished the year with a flourish, batting .275/.320/.626 with seven homers and 16 RBI over his final 24 games. Here's hoping that it was a one-year aberration rather than the start of an injury-prone reputation, but Merrill has a lot of rebound potential among players you'll find in the early-to-middle stages of your draft.

After a miserable, injury-marred 2024, Bichette rebounded last season with the same kind of elite-contact, line drive-oriented approach he exhibited during his 2021-23 peak -- only to see his regular season (and early postseason) interrupted by yet another injury, this time a knee sprain. It rekindled the durability question, which has sapped almost all of the above-average speed he once possessed. The Mets are banking on Bichette's per-game hitting numbers, which were excellent across five months, as being more representative of his skill set, and we tend to agree. Still, we'd understand if his injury risk causes you to balk at the cost of a top-50 overall pick.

Duran saw a decline in most areas in 2025 after his first All-Star season the year prior, losing nearly 30 points in batting average along with five homers and 10 steals from his 2024 totals. The outfielder still compiled valuable numbers with 16 HR and 24 SB across 157 regular-season games with the Red Sox while once again leading the American League in triples with 13. He also reached 40 doubles for the second consecutive year, with only Bobby Witt having more two-baggers over the last two seasons. Duran can fly, and his ability to take the extra base boosts his slugging percentage. The right-field dimensions at Fenway Park help the lefty hitter as well, though there have been rumors that Duran could eventually be traded. Even with the drop in performance and lingering uncertainty surrounding his future in Boston, Duran will remain a coveted piece in fantasy.

Yelich's 644 plate appearances last season marked his highest total since 2022, while his 29 home runs were his most since 2019. He wasn't quite able to reach 20 steals for a third straight season but was still productive on the basepaths with 16 thefts. He topped 100 RBI for just the second time in his career and finished with a .264/.343/.452 slash line in 150 games. Yelich saw more action than ever at designated hitter with just 19 appearances in the outfield -- which could limit his positional eligibility in 2026 -- and that's unlikely to change much going forward given the back issues he's dealt with throughout his time in Milwaukee. Now entering his age-34 season, Yelich's swing should continue to age well, but some modest regression wouldn't be surprising at this point in his career.

Busch is coming off a tremendous sophomore season which saw him flex his power to another level while improving his strikeout rate five full percentage points. Busch hit 30 of his 34 homers against righties and was quite neutralized by lefties all season, and he found road parks to be more conducive to his homers with 21 of the 34 coming away from Wrigley Field. Busch may also be one of the few players to hit 30 or more home runs in a season during which his most common position in the batting order was leadoff, as he led off for the Cubs in 52 contests last season. Should that usage continue, Busch is likely to score more runs than he drives in, but he did still manage 90 RBI last season. If he and Ian Happ flip in the projected lineup around Nico Hoerner, Busch could drive in 100-plus.
