Perez's return from April 2024 Tommy John surgery offered far more promise in terms of his underlying metrics than what his surface numbers indicated. Among pitchers with at least as many as his 20 starts, he ranked second in average fastball velocity (97.9 mph), fifth in BAA (.195) and 15th in strikeout rate (27.3%). Perez also finished the year with a flourish, averaging 16.0 fantasy points over his final four starts, further underscoring his growth potential heading into 2026. Expect the Marlins to be cautious with their 22-year-old, soon-to-be-ace, but he's one of the best upside picks among starting pitchers.

The active career leader in saves (476), Jansen's skills gradually eroded as he progressed through his mid-30s, but the Tigers see enough potential in him at age 38 that they signed him as their presumptive closer. He has saved at least 25 games in each of the past 13 uninterrupted MLB seasons, but 2025 saw him register career worsts in strikeout rate (24.4%), Statcast expected ERA (3.74) and hard-hit rate allowed (44.6%). Jansen is a role-driven, middle-of-your-staff type for fantasy purposes, the promise of save chances in Detroit buoying his value -- so long as he pitches effectively enough to keep the job.

Fairbanks remarkably avoided the injury bug in 2025 -- he had missed at least a month while on the IL in each of the previous four seasons -- and set personal bests with his 27 saves and 60 1/3 innings. While his raw stuff and underlying metrics, paled in comparison to his 2022-23 peak, he was plenty serviceable in the Rays' closer role. The Marlins, taking note of that and his 17 saves and 2.43 ERA away from homer-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, signed Fairbanks to handle their ninth inning, where he'll call a much more pitcher-friendly environment his home. Once the more durable, top-shelf relievers are off the board, this is a strong, risk/reward choice to fill out your pitching staff.

Wacha is coming off a season in which he threw the most innings he has worked since his 181.1 frames way back in 2015. Wacha has avoided the injured list the past two seasons and continues to provide consistent if boring production to fantasy managers with safe ratios and a below-average strikeout rate. Wacha has a deep repertoire of pitches built around his changeup, and he will throw all six pitches to both righties and lefties, using his abilities to keep hitters off balance to make up for what he lacks in velocity. This approach is a perfect fit for pitching in Kansas City where Wacha has allowed just 13 home runs since joining the club compared to 19 in his road starts. This season should be yet another consistently steady campaign for the veteran, but you will need to find your strikeouts from other pitchers.

Mize hit the injured list in May with a hamstring strain but still made his first All-Star team in 2025, going 9-3 with a 3.15 ERA and 1.22 WHIP over 88.2 innings with Detroit in the first half. He slumped to a 4.92 ERA and 1.34 WHIP after the break, mirroring the team's collective slide. The right-hander shaved his walk rate to just 5.7 percent while upping his strikeout rate to a career-high 22.2 percent last season, though he got touched up with the long ball on occasion, with the splitter in particular yielding a surprising number of homers. After being drafted No. 1 overall in 2018, Mize underwent Tommy John surgery in 2022, missing the entire 2023 season as a result. No ace but from a bust, Mize has re-emerged in recent years as a capable mid-rotation arm for the Tigers.

Alvarez has had an interesting past 12-18 months. The catcher suffered a hamate bone fracture in early March which delayed the start to his 2025 season, and then he was demoted to Triple-A after a slow .236/.319/.333 start which included struggles behind the plate. He returned with a vengeance just after the break and hit .276/.360/.561, reminding everyone of his potential even while playing through a sprained UCL in his right thumb. That UCL injury means he has needed surgery to repair the UCLs in both of his hands as well as the hamate bone fracture in the past year. His offseason preparation may once again be affected, but those second-half numbers remind us of the tremendous upside in this young man. The balance between risk and reward is the big question.

King made huge strides with both his control and command of what would otherwise be a lackluster fastball-sweeper combo last season, posting a 2.78 ERA and MLB’s ninth-most holds (27). Though he struggled to keep the ball in the yard (10 HR), he’s generally good enough at minimizing hard contact that he should improve in that department in 2026. Consider him a top source of holds, with fantasy-worthy ratios.

A submarining, ground ball-generating, righty-dominating short reliever, Rogers is one of the very best at his craft. However, you need to recognize the craft -- that of a locked-in, primary setup man rather than a flamethrower -- for what it is. He's a holds machine, owning 18% of the total number of 30-hold seasons across the past five seasons (he has four), with some of the most projectable ratios around. That's a nice thing to have in formats that reward setup men.

Fully recovered from June 2023 Tommy John surgery, deGrom in 2025 made more starts (30) and pitched more innings (172 2/3) than he had in any season since his back-to-back Cy Young seasons of 2018-19, remarkably doing so at the age of 37. He exhibited similarly elite average fastball velocity (97.5 mph) and whiff rate on his slider (39.0%), yet couldn't match the lofty strikeout rates, to those prime years. That's not unexpected from a pitcher at deGrom's age, and injury setbacks will remain a worry for the remainder of his career. An extreme fly-ball lean over his final 10 starts (an MLB-leading 42.1%) also heightens regression concerns. He still has what it takes to be a fantasy ace, but the steep downside present in his profile also makes him a dicey leading-man pick.

Much of the storyline surrounding Sanchez during last year's breakthrough was his second straight year of increased sinker velocity -- he went from 92.1 mph in 2023 to 94.5 in 2024 to 95.4 in 2025 -- but the real story was the advances he made with his changeup. He struck out 130 batters with that pitch alone, the most by any pitcher in six years. Sanchez dodged a minor scare with his elbow in April, swiftly rebounding to post more quality starts than any pitcher, as well as the third-best ERA from that point forward. His combination of pinpoint control, extreme ground ball repertoire and top-shelf stuff make him one of the safest investments on the pitching side (if there is such a thing in this modern age). Draft Sanchez as your fantasy ace with confidence.

Amidst a teardown in Minnesota, Ryan stood tall with a career-best 3.42 ERA over a career-high 171 innings in 2025. The right-hander was one of two Twins All-Stars, along with Byron Buxton. Ryan has emerged as one of the team's top starters over the last few seasons, though he could be on his way out in due time as the organization continues to rebuild. Ryan would be befitting of the ace label almost anywhere given that he ranks seventh among qualified starters in strikeout-minus-walk percentage over the last three seasons. Home runs and occasional injuries have held him back from reaching true greatness, but Ryan is only 29 and his best years may still be ahead of him. With six pitches and pinpoint control, Ryan can be drafted with confidence as an SP2 for fantasy leagues.

Just about everything that could possibly have gone wrong for Rutschman in 2025, his age-27 season, did. He hit just .203/.300/.332 across the first two months, made trips to the IL for both obliques (left in June, right in August) and was ultimately pressed for his job by top prospect Samuel Basallo. That competition is the biggest lingering issue, as both players appear likely to make the team in a catcher/DH combination for a team that has a lot of other DH alternatives. Rutschman was previously a budding points-league star thanks to his well-rounded offensive game and the promise of hefty DH time. With that no longer a guarantee, he needs a standout spring to rekindle a top-5 positional valuation in the format. That ceiling remains possible, considering his age and skill set, however.

Stanton didn't debut for the Yankees in 2025 until mid-June due to tendinitis in both elbows, but his presence was worth the wait as he posted 24 home runs and a .944 OPS, which was his best mark since his MVP campaign in 2017. He played in just 77 games but still provided plenty of run production with 66 RBI, though his actual runs total (36) was unsurprisingly much lower given his awful sprint speed. A 34.3 percent strikeout rate was the highest of Stanton's career, but he continues to hit the ball as hard as anyone in baseball. Expecting a repeat of that production over a larger sample wouldn't be wise, but Stanton has clubbed 24-plus homers each of the past five seasons and seems likely to do so again in 2026, even as he enters his age-36 season.

Elder's 5.30 ERA and 1.39 WHIP over 28 starts in 2025 are ugly on the surface, though his 2.82 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across his final seven starts provide some reason for optimism heading into 2026.  He cut down on the walks (2.9 BB/9) but also struck out fewer batters (7.5 K/9) compared to 2024. Atlanta will be looking to return to contention after a down year, and the right-hander may need to carry that late-season form into spring training in order to have a chance of making the Opening Day rotation. Regardless, Elder is likely to make some starts for Atlanta at some point in 2026, but his days could be numbered if he struggles early on.

O’Hearn has carved out a “strong side of a straight platoon” role over the past three seasons, batting .280/.346/.445 against righties in that time, which makes him one of the more useful late-round picks in fantasy leagues that allow daily transactions. His move to Pittsburgh, and pitcher-friendly PNC Park, does lower his prospective number of actionable matchups somewhat, but he’s someone to keep in mind as you round out your roster.

Williams took a sizable, statistical step forward in 2025, shaving more than a run and three-quarters off his ERA while reaching the 30-start plateau for the first time as a professional, but his skill set remained a bit of a mixed bag. He had the majors' worst qualified walk rate (11.8%), the widest negative ERA-FIP differential (-1.33) and poor metrics in terms of contact quality allowed, signaling regression coming due. Still, Williams is only 26 years old, equipped with a 96.6-mph fastball and a pair of elite breaking pitches (curveball, sweeper) that make him especially tough against lefties, giving him growth potential that could neutralize those luck factors. It's probably best to treat his draft stock similarly to his 2025 fantasy finishes: SP24 (points), SP28 (rotisserie).

Olson is a model of durability and elite power, even if his borderline MVP-candidate 2023 season now looks like an outlier. He hasn't missed a game since May 1, 2021, and is the only player with at least 29 home runs and .200 isolated power in each of the past seven full MLB seasons (2018-19, '21-25). As a heart-of-the-order hitter for a Braves lineup that feels like it has been stricken with exceedingly awful luck over the past two seasons, Olson seems a strong bet for another near-30 HR/100 RBI campaign, with the possibility of more power upside. He's worth selecting in the early rounds of any draft.

Suarez is coming off back-to-back top-10 fantasy closer seasons, his 76 saves during that time being MLB's most. However, let's address the elephant in the room following his departure from San Diego. He has an ERA nearly a full run higher away from Petco Park (3.41) than at it (2.44) for his career, with his other ratios reflecting a steep home/road split. Fortunately, Suarez's combination of high-90s average fastball velocity, elite control and balanced platoon splits should afford him a relatively soft landing in Atlanta's Truist Park -- a more hitter-friendly, but hardly heavenly, venue. Expect his ratios to rise, but as the Braves' clear closer, he should put forth another potential top-10 fantasy season at the position.

Lee put forth a second consecutive solid season in setup relief, his holds total swelling to a team-leading 19 in 2025. That he lowered his walk rate was a help, as that's one of the categorical fears among short relievers with the fly ball leaning he has (33.0 FB%). Lee should be one of the team's most trusted late-inning relievers again in 2026, though the addition of Robert Suarez, who should handle the eighth, might cap the lefty's holds ceiling around last year's total.

The Phillies have talked about wanting to utilize Marsh as an everyday outfielder rather than a platoon player since acquiring him in 2022, but his continued struggles against left-handed pitching (.577 OPS in 2025) have essentially made that impossible. The good news is that he continues to crush righties and posted a .300/.356/.482 slash line against them last season. His production on the basepaths dropped significantly with just seven steals after he posted a career-high 19 in 2024, and 11 home runs marked his lowest total since 2022 while his 43 RBI and 59 runs were also underwhelming. Marsh's ratios continue to be strong, but the lack of volume significantly caps his counting stats and limits his upside in most formats.

Carroll rebounded from a disappointing sophomore 2024 -- one in part caused by tweaks he made to his swing the preceding winter that threw off his rhythm -- to register a 30/30 season for the first time in his career. He has now exceeded 400 fantasy points in each of his three complete MLB years, testament to his extra-base ability with the bat and selectivity at the plate. Carroll's .282 isolated power was exceeded by only six other qualified hitters, and he set a personal best with both his fly-ball and Statcast Barrel rates. He'll play 2026 at a prime-age 25, but a broken hamate bone in February cast doubt upon his availability for Opening Day and might require some time to recapture his timing thereafter. Carroll is still capable of first-round fantasy production, but keep tabs on his recovery before spending one of the draft's very first picks on him.

Just 23 years old, Skenes is already authoring one heck of a career story. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 Draft, Skenes breezed to the majors after only 12 minor league starts and struck out 11 batters over six no-hit innings in his second career game on his way to winning the 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award. He also became the first player in history to start the All-Star Game in both of his first two seasons, won the 2025 NL Cy Young Award and posted the lowest ERA (1.99) of any pitcher through his first 46 career starts. If there's a nit to pick, it's that his Pirates provided him such little run support (3.38 runs, third worst among ERA qualifiers) that he won only 10 games despite leading the majors in ERA in 2025. But hey, they're at least a little better offensively entering 2026? Skenes is as good a bet as any to lead all pitchers in fantasy points as well as the Player Rater.

Fresh off a breakthrough 2024 that saw him finish fourth in AL MVP voting, Henderson suffered an intercostal strain five games into spring training that seemed to derail him for most of last year. While he returned to action eight days into the regular season, he never seemed to recapture his prior power stroke, posting a .748 OPS and seven home runs in his first 50 games and reflecting a 5% decrease in his fly-ball rate for the full year. Henderson did, however, maintain his former line-drive stroke as well as his elite speed, swiping a pro-best 30 bases. Perhaps the winter's rest will help him recapture his prior pop. He's a name to track during spring training, as he'll enter 2026 at 24 years old, with MVP-caliber upside if he has a strong showing.

Chourio's first two MLB seasons were almost spot-on as far as counting numbers are concerned. Often, fantasy managers might therefore assume the player has locked in that level of performance expectation, but in his case, remember that Chourio will begin 2026 only 21 years, 15 days old, and he showed glimpses of growth in 2025. His postseason -- .341/.362/.682 rates and four home runs in 12 games, despite dealing with hamstring issues -- was as compelling evidence as any, but he also reflected noticeable jumps in his bat speed and Barrel rate. Besides, he seemed to be turning the corner in early July before the hamstring problem first began. Chourio still has a path to superstardom and, while he's a potentially more profitable pick in rotisserie than points leagues, he's a player you shouldn't let last more than a few rounds in any draft.

Sean Murphy's cracked rib in March paved the way for Baldwin to step in as the Braves' Opening Day catcher, and despite Murphy's lingering presence all year, the lefty slugger made enough of his opportunity that he ultimately captured NL Rookie of the Year honors. Baldwin's is a rare combination of contact, contact quality and raw power. He joined fellow catcher Alejandro Kirk as baseball's only players with at least 400 plate appearances, 10% Statcast Barrel, 45% hard-hit and 80% contact rates. Baldwin also excelled against same-handed pitchers, his almost complete skill set diminishing the chances of a sophomore slump. Although Murphy remains in Atlanta, Baldwin should handle the bulk of the catching duties -- perhaps in a straight platoon, but that's still plenty to make him one of the position's top picks.

"Well?! We're waiting!" It might feel like forever to fantasy managers, but it's important to remember that Holliday, the No. 1 pick of the 2022 Draft and consensus No. 1 prospect entering his 2024 MLB debut season, is still only 22 years old and just 427 professional games removed from high school. Not all prospects blossom immediately, and perhaps he's one of those who takes baby steps to get there. Holliday's metrics were so-so at best in his first full big-league campaign in 2025, but he did greatly improve his patience (95th percentile chase rate) and contact (80th percentile rate) during the season's second half, and he showed hints of future five-category rotisserie potential. That said, a fractured right hamate bone suffered in February will cost him important spring training time and likely land him on the IL to start the season. Holliday is still a high-upside middle-round pick, but picking him requires a bit of a leap of faith.

Lodolo made huge strides in 2025, posting a 4.8% walk rate that ranked sixth among pitchers with at least 20 starts, while generating many swings-and-misses on pitches out of the zone -- he had the fourth-best chase rate among that same group -- before injuries largely interrupted his final two months. At the time, he had scored the 20th-most fantasy points among pitchers. Whether those injuries (a blister, an illness, a right groin issue) represent a recurring pattern is in question, but Lodolo could be on the verge of a full-season breakthrough with the adjustments he has made. He's a pitcher to watch during spring training, as he'd have a top-25 starter's ceiling with a standout March.

The Cardinals moved Contreras from catcher to first base last offseason, but the defensive move didn't bring significant change at the plate as he posted a .257/.344/.447 slash line with 20 home runs, 80 RBI and 70 runs in 135 games. A .791 OPS ended up being his worst mark since 2021, and that was largely fueled by his 8.2 percent walk rate, which was nearly five points worse than his 2024 mark. Being traded from the rebuilding Cardinals to the Red Sox in December should provide Contreras with the potential for more run production in 2026, especially since Fenway Park is more hitter friendly to right-handed bats than Busch Stadium. Contreras has a pretty well established floor with an average of 20 home runs, 59 RBI, 60 runs and a .252 batting average across the past five seasons, so he's a fairly safe mid-tier fantasy target.

Stewart is an MLB-ready hitter with growing power who merely needs a defensive place to play. He hit five homers across an 18-game "cup of coffee" with the Reds, playing more at first base than at third, but he'll probably be in the spring mix at both spots due to the team's injury question marks at those positions, although Eugenio Suarez's addition hurt his chances for everyday at-bats. Stewart hit .309/.383/.524 with 20 homers and 17 steals in 118 games between Double-A Chattanooga and Triple-A Louisville last season, and he'll have the Reds' homer-friendly ballpark helping his cause. He's a late-round flier in redrafts as is, and a solid dynasty building block as well.

Albies had a season to forget in 2025 with a career-low .671 OPS across 157 games with Atlanta. Adding injury to insult, Albies suffered a hamate bone fracture in his left hand during the final week. He is expected to be fully recovered in time for spring training, but the second baseman's inconsistency in recent years makes him tough to trust entering 2026. Historically, Albies has done a disproportionate amount of his damage from the right side of the plate -- his struggles from the left side have led to calls for him to give up switch hitting. An All-Star as recently as 2023, Albies has shown little in recent years to justify enduring optimism, though at least the downward trends have not yet extended to his overall strikeout rate. Further, the 29-year-old still provides efficiency on the basepaths.

Burleson cut his chase rate down and saw immediate results in 2025, slashing .290/.343/.459 across 139 games with the Cardinals to win the Silver Slugger at the utility spot. He improved against lefties and led the team in OPS on the strength of improved patience and selectivity, though he ended up falling short of his 2024 totals in home runs, runs, RBI and steals due to missing time in the second half with a wrist injury. With Willson Contreras now in Boston, Burleson will take over as the everyday first baseman in St. Louis after splitting time between the outfield (74 games), first base (50 games) and DH (22 games) last season. The profile does not look out of place in the middle of a major-league lineup, and entering his age-27 campaign, Burleson still appears capable of more.

Clement ended up being a key contributor for the Blue Jays throughout 2025, batting .277 with 35 doubles, 50 RBI and 83 runs in 157 games. He hit just nine home runs and stole six bags, both of which were drops from 2024 when he recorded 12 apiece. He makes a ton of contact and had low strikeout and walk rates (10.4 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively). Clement played in at least 29 games at third base, second base and shortstop while also making 15 appearances at first, which is more playing time than a utility player usually gets. Clement doesn't really profile as a true lineup regular, and he could be pushed out of a starting role, depending who else the Blue Jays sign this winter. He can have some deep-league appeal due to the high average, run potential and defensive versatility but likely won't get enough volume to be a reliable fantasy contributor.

Injuries again marred Moreno's season, as he appeared in fewer than 100 games for the second straight year. He was batting .270/.324/.414 in mid-June when he was finally placed on the IL after being hit in the hand two weeks earlier. The fractured finger sidelined him for more than two months, and after returning he posted an impressive .311/.397/.466 line over 30 games. For the season, he set new personal bests in barrel and hard-hit rate while hitting more flyballs to drive power. That came at the cost of a higher strikeout rate, though it remained well below average. Moreno's typically strong defense graded as league average, but he played fewer games behind the plate, especially down the stretch when he often served as the DH. It's unclear how much of last season's gains will carry over, and durability remains a concern.

After a three-year run as the Yankees' closer and seven years in MLB as a reliever, Holmes signed with the Mets as a starter in December of 2024 and held his own last season in his first year as a full-time starter. The right-hander had his workload managed down the stretch but finished 2025 with a 3.53 ERA, 1.30 WHIP and 129:66 K:BB across 165.2 innings (33 appearances). His move to the rotation predictably resulted in reduction in velocity and strikeouts, but Holmes was able to mostly offset that by being one of the most prolific groundball starters in baseball (55.9 percent groundball rate). A 7.0 K/9 certainly lowers Holmes' upside, but he'll still have a fair amount of fantasy value if he can replicate his run prevention from 2025.

Whether due to injuries or the aging process, Trout is no longer the perennial MVP candidate he once was. Though he played 130 games in 2025 -- more than he had in the previous two seasons combined or in any single year since 2019 -- he hit just .232 with his lowest OPS in any full year (.797). Trout no longer catches up with breaking stuff at his prior Hall of Fame levels, leading to high strikeout totals and lower batting averages, though his power remains excellent (.207 ISO and 93rd-percentile Statcast Barrel rate). The result is a player now similarly valued in roto and points leagues, one now best left to filling out your lineup rather than leading it.

Happ is entering the final year of his most recent contract, which is something to keep in mind for those who like factors such as contract years when targeting players. Happ has been a consistent on-base machine in recent seasons, but his batting average is now league average as the rest of the league has come down to his level. The switch hitter is at his best when facing righties as most of his homers come from the left side, but he has held his own hitting from the right side of the plate as well in recent years. His on-base abilities lock him in somewhere near the top of the Chicago lineup for 2026, but it will be a different batting order without the presence of Kyle Tucker, and the club's apparent reticence to spend big to replace him. Happ has been a 20/80/80/.240 producer for three straight years and expect a fourth.

For a pitcher to possess as stuff as filthy as Miller's is flat-out unfair. Among those who have thrown at least 400 of either pitch in any of the 18 seasons for which we have pitch data, Miller's 101.2-mph average fastball velocity last season was second highest, while his 54.6% whiff rate with his slider was 15th. Though his deadline deal to the Padres bumped him from his prior closer role, he thrived in setup relief with his new team, scoring the sixth-most fantasy points (124) despite not winning a game and posting only two saves in that time. Robert Suarez's winter departure paved the way for Miller to reclaim the ninth-inning role in San Diego, from which the right-hander has a wide-open path to being the top performing relief pitcher in fantasy baseball in 2026.

Bellinger's skill set is a cavalcade of underlying metric-busting magic. Here are his percentile rankings in various Statcast metrics over the past three seasons combined: 21st in bat speed, 25th in hard-hit rate and 39th in Barrel rate. Nevertheless, Bellinger's three-year averages during that same time are a .281 batting average, 24 homes, 91 RBI and 14 steals -- and he has even earned MVP votes in two of those seasons! Having as elite a contact rate as he does certainly helps, as does his extreme fly ball leaning (which makes him a particularly good fit for Yankee Stadium). Bellinger isn't the MVP example he was in 2019, but he's a plenty useful fantasy player all around, and a near-star in points leagues.

Through 15 starts, Sale was on track to defend his 2024 Cy Young, carrying a 2.52 ERA and 1.16 WHIP with 114 strikeouts across 89.1 innings before a fractured left ribcage sidelined him for a little more than 10 weeks. He returned without missing a beat, logging a 2.72 ERA and 0.83 WHIP over his final six starts and striking out 51 in 36.1 frames. On the season, the underlying skills remained elite, as his 26.1 strikeout-minus-walk percentage ranked fourth among pitchers with at least 120 innings. While the injury underscores the health risk attached to the left-hander entering his age-37 season, the fact that it was not arm-related has kept early drafters confident, with Sale still among the first 10 starters selected.

A first-half flexor strain limited Gilbert to just 25 starts spanning 131 innings, breaking his streak of three straight seasons with at least 185 frames. The injury interrupted his best season ever, at least in terms of his ERA estimators. His actual ERA ran a little higher than expected despite Gilbert setting a new personal best with a 32.3 percent strikeout rate. Gilbert's 26.5 K-BB percentage was the third highest among all pitchers logging at least 130 innings. That jump came after he shelved his cutter in favor of more four-seamers, splitters and sliders, though the adjusted mix led to a modest uptick in walks. Even so, Gilbert enters the season as a key piece of one of the league's top rotations, pitching roughly half his games in the most favorable park for pitchers.

One of the best control specialists in baseball, Kirby's 2025 was sidetracked by shoulder inflammation that cost him most of spring training and nearly two regular-season months. He'd rebound with 11 quality starts, a 3.59 ERA and 4.95 K/BB ratio over his final 17 starts -- and he was productive in three of his four postseason starts. All of this offers encouragement for a 2026 rebound. Kirby's 3.6% walk rate over his first four MLB seasons is the second lowest by any pitcher in the modern era, and he has an underrated slider that's capable of generating strikeouts. There's risk here, but the prospective reward would easily place him among his position's top 10 performers.

From a rates perspective, Diaz's 2025 was up there alongside any of his best statistical seasons, including his outrageous, 57-save 2018. The main drawback was his garnering only 31 save chances -- an inexplicably low total for a closer from an 83-win team. Diaz departed the Mets during the winter for a Dodgers team that has finished second in the majors in save chances in both of the last two seasons, despite their never truly having a singular ninth-inning choice over that time. While manager Dave Roberts could exploit a matchup every now and then, Diaz's contract and raw stuff almost assuredly will earn him the role for 2026, from which the right-hander is as good a bet to top his position in fantasy value as anyone.

Freeman is aging like a fine California wine even if he is no longer playing every single game in a season. His days of 100-plus runs and 100-plus RBI appear to be over as his power is waning in his mid-30s, but he is still one of the few five-category producers at his position. He was able to hit .295 last year despite his strikeout rate surging to its highest level since his 2016 season after a long trend of Freeman having one of the better rates in the league. Ideally, Freeman would get some half days at DH, but that is not an option on the Dodgers. Instead, he gets to enjoy hitting behind Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts and in front of Will Smith, Max Muncy and Tesocar Hernandez. His 2024-2025 production is very repeatable with his skills and lineup spot, but don't get greedy.

Hoerner is that rare type of player who always seems to surprise fantasy managers with his year-end grades. He's a noted points-league standout, thanks to his elite contact skills -- he's one of just three players with at least an 85% qualified contact rate in all of the last three seasons. He also has a penchant for doubles and frequent appearances in the upper third of the Cubs lineup. However, Hoerner is also a successful rotisserie player, in that hitters capable of a .300 batting average and 30 stolen bases are a rarity nowadays -- there have only been six such seasons over the past four years, whereas there were six of them alone as recently as 2006. He should be regarded as a near-foundational piece in points leagues, in part due to how thin second base is. Just understand that if you take him early in a rotisserie league, you'll need to make up for his power shortcomings elsewhere on your roster.

Fried settled in nicely in his first year in pinstripes, setting personal bests in wins (19), starts (32), innings pitched (195 1/3) and strikeouts (189). He performed consistently excellent outside of an eight-start, July/early August stretch in which his control wavered (6.80 ERA, 8.3 BB%). These days, that's the description of a fantasy ace, as few pitchers are spared the occasional wart, and most have similar, minor injury questions to what's in Fried's past. He's one of the higher-floor options at the position, and one of the few pitchers who, health willing, seems likely to exceed the 200-IP threshold. Build your staff around him with confidence.

After two seasons of his elite velocity and swing-and-miss skills toiling in a closer's timeshare in manager Scott Servais' matchups-oriented bullpen, Munoz thrived as the Mariners' full-time guy in Dan Wilson's first full season calling the shots. Munoz finished second in fantasy points among relief pitchers, third in saves and fourth in ERA, not to mention he added 8 1/3 shutout innings and two saves in the Mariners' two-round playoff run. He'll return in the same role, for a similarly competitive team, meaning another run as a top-five fantasy closer seems likely.

A model of consistency, durability and elevated floors among pitchers, Valdez hit a rough patch over 2025's final two months, which could explain why he lingered on the free agent market for so long. A .330 BABIP and 60.8 LOB% hinted that his 6.05 ERA during that time was more mirage than trend, while the left-hander's 83 quality starts, 767 2/3 innings pitched and 1,659 fantasy points from 2022-25 combined (all of which ranked top-three at his position) provide fairer perspective on his skills. As an extreme ground baller, Valdez's only team-influenced effect would be the infield defense behind him. The Tigers’ group is strong enough to assure him another potential top-15 fantasy starter stat line.

A Will Smith won another World Series, but Smith is more than just a funny trivia question. He has been a force at the catching position for fantasy managers these past few seasons, even as he lost some of the volume this past year as the designated hitter spot on the roster was re-occupied by Shohei Ohtani. Smith was on pace to best his 2024 production despite the reduction in plate appearances and also went on to post a career-best batting average in 2025. If anything, one could argue the reduced volume was a good thing for Smith to keep him fresh over the course of a full season under the physical demands of catching. This season should be more of the same for playing time and production with a step back toward his career level for batting average with batted-ball luck coming back to previous norms.

Two-pitch guys are supposed to be relievers and not starters, but Gausman never got that message as he continues to ride his heavy fastball-splitter approach to continued success as a major-league starter. Gausman's 2025 saw him work a career high in regular-season innings along with another 30 stressful postseason innings which might be a cause for concern heading into 2026 (see Zac Gallen from 2023 to 2024). Over the past five seasons, Gausman is one of just three pitchers with at least 1000 strikeouts and is tied for second in games started while also being second in innings pitched. Everything looks good for his skills, but workhorses eventually stop being workhorses, so proceed with a degree of caution.

By a show of hands, who had Pages finishing with the second-most home runs on the Dodgers, trailing only Shohei Ohtani? Exactly. Pages provided stability for a roster dealing with injuries throughout the season, appearing in 156 games, mostly in center field, while showing off one of the strongest outfield arms in the league. Pages' chase rate is elevated, but he struck out at a near-league-average rate last season, suggesting improved swing decisions could allow him to rely less on pulled flyballs and more on hitting the ball with greater authority. Stolen-base efficiency remains a concern, as Pages was caught seven times in 21 attempts, and continued issues could earn him the red light.

Nimmo put together another productive campaign in 2025, slugging 25 homers with 92 RBI, both career highs, to go along with 81 runs and 13 steals across 155 games with the Mets. Last season marked his fourth straight reaching 150 games, as Nimmo continues to distance himself from the injury issues that plagued him earlier in his career. In November, he was traded to the Rangers amidst rumors of a rift with former teammate Francisco Lindor, a move that looks like a wash for Nimmo in many respects. The outfielder gave up a bit in terms of OBP and was more aggressive in recent years as he took on more of a run-producer role, but he has the plate skills to transition back to leadoff duty if Texas prefers to go that route.

After hitting 232 home runs across a seven-year span (2018-24) in Japan, Okamoto suffered an elbow injury in a collision at first base, limiting him to a career-low 77 games. Ah, but what productive games they were! He hit .322/.411/.581 and made contact 87% of the time -- all of those career-best rates -- which bodes well for a smooth transition to the U.S. game. Okamoto figures to slide in at third base for the Blue Jays, where he'll benefit from hitting in the middle-to-lower portion of their deep lineup. As is the case with any Japanese hitter, his range of outcomes is wide due to the adjustment period required, but he's a well-rounded hitter who brings a lot of fantasy upside in the late rounds.

There are five-tool talents, and then there's Witt. He was one of just two players to register at least 90th percentile Statcast metrics in terms of expected weighted on-base average (xwOBA), sprint speed and outs above average defensively (Corbin Carroll was the other) -- and Witt was the only one to also register at least a 90th percentile expected batting average. It's a skill set that solidifies his universal first-round fantasy status, and he'll enter 2026 at a prime-age 25. That his Royals moved the fences in at Kauffman Stadium this season can only help Witt's power prospects, as a return to the 30/30 form he displayed in 2023 and 2024 could be coming.

After a rocky first year in the U.S., year number two for Yamamoto was consistently excellent from start to finish -- literally. He won both the season's first game (in Japan in March) and its last, Game 7 of the World Series. In sum, he posted top-6 numbers across the league in ERA, WHIP and strikeout rate. Yamamoto's innings spike, totaling 211 frames between the regular season and postseason after 112 2/3 the year before, represents a slight concern following the rotator cuff issues he experienced in 2023, but his Dodgers are as careful with managing pitchers as any team in baseball. He's a fantasy ace and should be drafted in the opening rounds as such.

A dominating ninth-inning force in Minnesota for 3.5 seasons, Duran's career truly took off following his deadline deal to the Phillies last July. Finally bestowed with a ninth-inning role all his own, the right-hander saved an MLB-leading 16 games for his new team, all the while maintaining his top-shelf, closer-caliber raw stuff. Duran returns in the same role for a competitive 2026 Phillies team, giving him a legitimate chance to contend for the fantasy points/Player Rater lead at his position. His combination of a 100-plus-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve make him one of the most attractive relief pitchers in drafts.

Gifted with a high-90s fastball, blossoming sweeper and some of the most pinpoint control of anyone in baseball, Woo broke through in a big way in 2025. He finished fifth among pitchers in fantasy points, third in WHIP and K/BB ratio, fourth in quality starts (21) and fifth in wins. Perhaps most importantly, he remained healthy for long enough to make a career-high 30 starts. A pectoral strain in September limited his contributions during the team's playoff run, but the winter's rest should afford him the chance to heal and merely warrants a quick glance once spring training opens. Woo is a legitimate fantasy ace.

Oblique issues sent Langford to the IL on three separate occasions in 2025, obstructing what was otherwise a solid step forward by him in his sophomore season. He was one of 16 players with at least 22 home runs and stolen bases, and he reflected noticeable gains in terms of Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates, while finishing in the 85th percentile in line-drive rate. Now 24, Langford could be ready to come into his own, though better luck in the health department will certainly play a part. He's an early-to-mid round pick with upside in all formats.

After finishing third in the majors in stolen bases in 2024, effectively a two-category player (steals and runs), Garcia went all Willie Mays Hayes-in-�Major League 2� last season, inexplicably trading his speed in the quest for power. He attempted only one stolen base across his final 44 games and just five over his final 79, while more than doubling his home run total for the full season. That's not to knock Garcia's improvements as he made huge strides with his selectivity and contact and saw a decent bump in terms of contact quality. We'd, of course, prefer to see him capitalize upon his career best .351 OBP with bushels of steals, which would make him more of an early-round target in rotisserie leagues. As is, he's a solid mid-round pick as he enters his age-26 season.

Coming off a 6.14 ERA and an unremarkable spring, Palencia opened the season at Triple-A Iowa before being recalled in mid-April to add bullpen depth. He quickly impressed, posting a 1.20 ERA and 0.80 WHIP with 15 strikeouts across 15 innings, which earned him a save opportunity amid struggles from Ryan Pressly and an injury to Porter Hodge. Though he blew his first chance, Palencia converted his next five save opportunities and retained the job until a shoulder injury sidelined him in early September. He returned for the final week in lower-leverage work. With the Cubs adding quality setup options, Palencia has a clear path to build on last year's team-leading 23 saves. While his track record is lacking, a repeat performance could elevate him into a higher tier.

A 31-year-old journeyman, O'Brien added velocity to his sinker and spin to his slider and broke through for the 2025 Cardinals, ultimately earning himself their closer job in the month of September. That might give him a leg up in their spring competition for the role, and his ground ball leaning and ability to suppress hard contact does minimize the downside if he emerges. Monitor O'Brien's spring progress, which will ultimately decide whether holds or saves are his target, but there's enough opportunity here to make him a viable fantasy late-rounder.

Jung was limited to just 46 games in 2024 due to a wrist injury, but he was able to stay mostly healthy last season and played in a career-high 131 contests. Unfortunately for fantasy managers, his offensive production still took a hit, and he finished 2025 with a .251 average, 14 homers and a career-low .390 slugging percentage. The Rangers demoted Jung to the minors for a few weeks over the summer, and he did fare a bit better the rest of the way with a .732 OPS, but he was still far from a consistent contributor. The power potential is obvious given the 23 homers that Jung launched as a rookie in 2023, but injuries and inconsistency have made him a volatile fantasy option with a seemingly low floor.

Castillo has outpitched his peripherals since joining the Mariners in 2022, and it may be by design rather than just good fortune. With the Reds, Castillo was an extreme groundball pitcher which helped offset the homer-friendly Great American Ball Park. In the Pacific Northwest, he is leaning more on his four-seam fastball, which generates more flyballs. T-Mobile Park suppresses home runs, so while his home-run rate has risen, it remains reasonable, and the added flyballs are driving a BABIP between .267 and .285 over the past four seasons. The change in approach has sent his strikeout rate into freefall, denting his fantasy allure and increasing his dependence on a low BABIP, a slippery slope. Entering his age-33 season, Castillo's floor is more wobbly than usual, and without strikeouts, the ceiling is limited.

Soler was limited to 82 games in 2025 due to back issues, which resulted in two trips to the injured list and cost him the final two months of the season. The veteran slugger wasn't particularly productive when available, finishing with 12 home runs, 34 RBI, 31 runs and a .215/.293/.387 slash line in 314 plate appearances. Soler is now entering his age-34 season, so the recurring back issues in 2025 could spell trouble moving forward, especially since he already wasn't the most consistent of hitters. Still, he's just two seasons removed from clubbing 36 homers for Miami, and he played in at least 137 games in both 2023 and 2024. Soler can't be fully written off despite the age and injury concerns.

One of four players in history with four 50-homer seasons, and one of three to hit 50-plus homers while winning the batting title (Jimmie Foxx, 1938; Mickey Mantle, 1956), Judge is baseball's preeminent all-around hitter. He has claimed three of the past four AL MVP awards, covering a span during which he hit .311 with an average of 53 home runs, 116 RBI, 118 runs scored and 114 walks per year. Now 33, Judge has also sufficiently answered the injury question that plagued him earlier in his career, as he has appeared in at least 152 games in three of the past four years, while batting .305/.473/.634 with 16 homers across his final 49 regular-season contests following a 10-day IL stint for an elbow issue in July/August. He's an exemplary choice to begin your draft in any fantasy format.

Don't let the persistent trade rumors swirling around him dissuade you that Skubal is as good a choice to lead your fantasy pitching staff as anyone. He's coming off back-to-back Cy Youngs, and has made consistent, notable improvements in almost every statistical category across his six MLB seasons. Skubal set personal bests in ERA, WHIP, walk rate, K/BB rate, whiff rate and rate of hard contact allowed in 2025. Since July 1, 2023, he has a 2.37 ERA and MLB-leading totals in both wins (38) and strikeouts (571). He's also entering his contract year -- the very reason for said trade rumors -- which, while hardly a guarantee as a motivating factor, assures he'll play 2026 at full bore, and with a team that will provide him the necessary support to again thrive.

One of the league's best young power/speed threats, De La Cruz was one of only five players with as many as 50 home runs and 75 steals between the date of his MLB debut (June 6, 2023) and the end of last July -- and the only one with as many as 100 steals over that stretch. Unfortunately, he struggled mightily over the season's final two months, batting just .221/.280/.341 with three homers and eight steals (in 10 attempts) over 52 games, likely as a result of his playing through a partially torn quadriceps. The winter's rest should afford De La Cruz time to sufficiently heal, but his funk served as a reminder that his free-swinging nature at the plate deepens his statistical downside, not to mention is significantly more useful in rotisserie than points-based leagues. To that point, he finished 17th on the 2024 Player Rater, but only 50th in fantasy points scored, so keep that disparity in mind as you weigh your investment in a rebound.

Turner had back-to-back healthy seasons in 2022 and 2023, but he has hit the injured list both of the two past years, with a hamstring injury at fault in 2025. Turner was still eighth overall in stolen bases despite the hamstring injury, and he remains one of the fastest players in baseball. On some teams, Turner would run every time he reached base, but he also hits in front of Kyle Schwarber and the Phillies do not frequently wish to open up first base and instead rely upon the threat of the steal to help Schwarber see more fastballs. Turner would have scored 100-plus runs had he avoided the injury and is likely thrilled Schwarber is returning to the club. The injury risk is the only thing holding Turner back from being a first-round pick.

A quadriceps injury he suffered in May derailed what was, at the time, a borderline MVP-caliber start to Bregman's Red Sox career. On May 14, for example, he was sixth among hitters in fantasy points, with significantly better contact-quality metrics than he had displayed in any prior year. Bregman never really recovered at the plate following his mid-July return, though his 154-game average over the three previous seasons (2022-24) suggests his finish was more aberration than the norm. The Cubs seemed to agree by granting him a five-year, $175 million guarantee, where they'll slot him high in what's a solid lineup. It's a good fit for Bregman, who is a great, building-block type of pick in points leagues thanks to his plate discipline and penchant for extra-base hits.

Iglesias finished one save shy of his third straight 30-save season, largely due to early-season struggles that led to a temporary demotion from the closer role in early June. He carried a 6.75 ERA and 1.54 WHIP on June 5 after blowing his fourth save. Following five scoreless outings spanning four innings, with two holds and a win, Iglesias reclaimed primary closing duties. He then posted a 1.37 ERA and 0.69 WHIP the rest of the way, converting 21 of 22 save chances. While ERA swings are often variance-driven, Iglesias leaned more heavily on his four-seamer in the second half while nearly shelving his slider, which helped address the home-run issues from earlier in the season. Atlanta signed the veteran to a one-year, $16 million deal, ostensibly to close, but the team also added last year's saves leader, Robert Suarez.

Estevez is coming off a fantastic season for Kansas City which saw him lead all of baseball with 42 saves for an 82-win club. Any concerns the talented Lucas Erceg would steal saves were quickly set aside as Estevez refused to give up any ground in the bullpen. He does not have the big strikeout rates of other closers in the game, but over the past two seasons, Estevez has the third-lowest ERA of all active closers and does not get himself into trouble with walks or homers. The fact Kansas City plays in a high rate of late and close games due to an inconsistent offense only helps Estevez get the ball on a regular basis. Estevez is not the sexiest closer, but he gets the job done and he should one again save 30-plus contests in 2026.

Imanaga is back with the Cubs for 2026 despite the team declining his three-year club option, since the club still tagged him with the qualifying offer, which ultimately led to the pitcher accepting it to re-prove his market viability next offseason. Imanaga had a hamstring injury in early May which kept him off the mound for six weeks. He made 20 starts before September and recorded eight wins with a 3.08 ERA, and 0.93 WHIP. However, his final five starts in September included a 6.51 ERA with velocity decline and 10 homers allowed in just 27.1 innings of work. Despite the decent overall numbers, his strikeout numbers dropped significantly to 7.3 K/9. The motivation is there for a great 2026, but are the skills?

The Astros thought they had solved their problems at first base when they signed Walker to a three-year, $60 million contract in December of 2024, but he mostly ended up just being the club's latest headache. The veteran first baseman struggled out of the gate with a .210/.273/.357 slash line through the first two months of the season, and he was never quite able to dig out of that hole. Walker showed signs of life in July and August with an .831 OPS, but that type of production was the expectation for the full season, not just two months. He still launched 27 home runs -- his fourth straight year with at least 26 -- and had respectable RBI (88) and run (72) totals, but the lack of consistency was a major issue. Walker is a decent candidate to bounce back in 2026, with his power and run production providing a solid floor despite the fact he's coming off a disappointing season.

Diaz's wRC+ declined for the second straight season despite a gain in power. Over the prior two years, his batting average closely tracked his xBA, but last season he finished 16 points below expected, driven largely by an unusually low line-drive BABIP. He also posted a career-low hard-hit rate, working against batting average. Added loft did push his barrel rate to a career high, and he paired that with the lowest strikeout rate of his career. Diaz grades as a below-average defender, so reversing the offensive slide will be important if he is to remain among the most heavily used backstops after his 567 plate appearances ranked sixth among catcher-eligible players last season. More line drives falling in would help, but he also needs to hit the ball with more authority and with greater selectivity.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 Draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2025 rookie season, Crews put forth solid power (7 HR) and speed (11 SB) numbers across his first 45 games, though his free-swinging nature (27.7 K%) led to a miserable, .196 batting average. An oblique strain would then cost him nearly three months, after which point he delivered more of the same, but with the same 50%-plus ground ball rate that must improve for him to truly realize his full power potential. Crews should get a long look for a starting role during spring training and, as he matures, he'll at least provide a solid stolen bases total for roto managers. He's more of a profitable late-rounder there than in points leagues, though he still has a high long-term ceiling for any fantasy format.

Coming off what was a top-10 fantasy starter's 2024, Miller's follow-up campaign was effectively ruined by bone spurs in his elbow, the ailment sending him to the IL twice and nearly doubling his ERA. Though his fastball velocity and whiff rate on his splitter improved over the season's final six weeks, his ERA over that time was nevertheless 5.62 and he couldn't find consistency at any point all year. Miller did avoid offseason surgery, but only spring training can demonstrate whether the winter's rest has helped him. He still has that ace-caliber stuff when healthy, so a strong spring would make him a potentially profitable late-round pick.

The AL’s leading base stealer in both of the last two seasons, Caballero has the look of a single-category, roto-angled standout -- until you look closer. He improved his plate approach and the resulting walk rate (12.7%) last year, demonstrated above-average defense at five different positions (while also appearing in a sixth, in center field) and gave the Yankees reasonable cause to let him push Anthony Volpe for their starting shortstop job this spring. Caballero’s skill set indeed is better suited for roto play, where he’s a strong mid-round pick for his steals, but a standout March could make him a potential breakout candidate.

A throwback type thanks to his elite-contact, batting average-but-minimal-pop hitting style, Arraez was a relative disappointment in 2025. He fell 12 points short of what would’ve been a fourth consecutive National League batting title, and the Padres struggled to find defensive positions at which to slot him due to his deficiencies in that regard. Teams might’ve seen similar issues with Arraez when considering him as a free-agent target, though the Giants ultimately saw enough in him to make him their everyday second baseman and probable No. 2 hitter. He’ll remain an underrated points league pick in that role, perhaps even from within the top 100 tier, while stabilizing roto teams’ batting averages.

The Dodgers repeated as champions, but Hernandez did not contribute to the same level during the 2025 regular season as the Regression Monster caught up to him. He spent time on the injured list in May with an adductor strain and also missed time after fouling a pitch off his foot. Ultimately, he lost eight homers, 10 RBI and seven steals from his 2024 totals, along with more than 100 points in OPS. The slugger was still a net positive but only slightly due to his deteriorating defense in right field. With Shohei Ohtani taking up the DH spot, Hernandez has to play the outfield to remain in the Los Angeles lineup. For now, he projects to remain a regular, but his poor defense at 33 years old leaves open some downside risk in regards to playing time.
